text: Beans, as grown and eaten in Nigeria, mostly means cowpea. It's a legume, and its seeds are a big source of protein for millions of people. Popular Nigerian varieties include Ewa Oloyin (honey beans), white/iron beans, and the newer PBR (pest-resistant) cowpea. Cowpea grows well in hot, dry parts of the world, including much of Africa. It copes with dry weather better than many other beans and legumes, which is why it does so well in places other crops struggle. Beans aren't just food — they're also useful to farmers for other reasons: They feed themselves nitrogen: beans pull nitrogen from the air and, with help from bacteria in the soil, turn it into food for the next crop planted there. They help the soil and cut down pests: growing beans breaks up the pest and disease problems that build up when you plant the same crop over and over, and their roots loosen up the soil. They pay off fast: many varieties are ready to harvest quickly, dried beans keep well without a fridge, and their short growing time means you can fit in an extra planting. They handle dry spells: beans cope with drought better than maize, and farmers often grow them alongside taller crops for shade.

In Nigeria, when people talk about the history of beans, they really mean the history of cowpea. It's an African crop that farmers here have grown for thousands of years, and it grew from a simple survival food into the protein Nigerians rely on most. Nigeria now grows and eats more cowpea than anywhere else in the world. 
### Long Before Colonial Times ###
 Cowpea first came from southern Africa, but West Africa is where it really took hold, and farmers here have grown it for thousands of years. Early farmers planted beans together with millet, sorghum, and yam, because they noticed beans kept the soil healthy for the other crops. Beans also became part of everyday culture — Ekuru, a steamed bean pudding among the Yoruba, and Akidi, a small native bean in the southeast, go back generations. 
### Crossing the Atlantic ###
 When enslaved West Africans were taken across the Atlantic, they carried cowpea seeds with them. That's how the crop reached the Americas, where it became known as the black-eyed pea. Nigeria's own Akara (bean fritters) traveled too, and became Acarajé, a well-loved street food in Bahia, Brazil. 
### After Independence, Into the 1980s ###
 Between 1961 and 1995, bean farming in Nigeria grew massively — production went up by around 441%. States like Borno, Kano, Sokoto, and Bauchi in the north became known as Nigeria's bean belt, thanks to their dry climate and wide farmland. In the 1960s, immigrants from Benin Republic and Togo brought a soft, mashed bean dish with a spicy palm-oil sauce to Lagos — that became Ewa Agoyin, now a Lagos favorite. Around the same time, Ewa Oloyin (honey beans) grew popular for its mild sweetness, used in porridge, Moi-Moi, and Akara. 
### Today ###
 The Dawanau Market in Kano is now the biggest agricultural market in West Africa, where huge amounts of beans grown in the north are gathered and sent out across the country and beyond. Because pests like the Maruca pod borer were destroying so much of the harvest, Nigerian scientists worked with IITA to develop PBR cowpea, a pest-resistant variety that lets farmers get good yields while spraying far less.

### Climate ###
 Beans like it warm — between 20°C and 32°C is ideal. Below 15°C slows growth, and above 40°C while the plant is flowering can make the flowers drop. They need moderate rain, around 500 mm to 1,200 mm over the season, and handle dry spells well once they're established. The most important thing is dry weather at harvest time — rain while the pods are filling or drying can rot the pods and ruin the seeds. Many local varieties only start flowering once the days get shorter, which is why planting later in the year (August/September) works better in the Middle Belt and South. 
### Soil ###
 Beans do best in well-drained sandy loam or clay loam soil. They really don't like wet feet — even two days of standing water can cause root rot, so avoid heavy clay that holds water. A slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 5.5–6.5) works best. If the soil is too acidic (below pH 5.0), the bacteria beans need to fix nitrogen can't do their job. Flat or gently sloping land is best. On a slope, plant across it rather than up and down, so heavy rain doesn't wash away the roots. 
### Where Beans Grow Best in Nigeria ###
 Far North (Sahel/Sudan Savanna): excellent for beans, though the rainy season is short and drought can hit suddenly — early-maturing varieties (about 60 days) work well here. Middle Belt (Guinea Savanna): very good for beans, but the humidity brings more pests — sticking closely to a spraying schedule matters here. Southern Rainforest Zone: only okay, and mostly seasonal — heavy rain and waterlogging are the challenge, so plant late (August/September) on raised ridges.

Getting the land ready is about giving bean roots a loose bed to grow into, letting water soak in easily, and clearing out weeds before the seeds even go in. 
### Clearing the Land ###
 Cut down bush and tall grass and clear the debris away rather than burning it — burning destroys the goodness in the topsoil. Also dig out old tree stumps and roots, especially if you'll be using a tractor, since hidden stumps can wreck the machinery. 
### Ploughing ###
 Plough soon after the first rains, once the soil is moist but not muddy, going down about 15 to 20 cm. This buries old weeds so they rot into the soil, and loosens it up so bean roots can go deep. 
### Harrowing ###
 About 7 to 10 days after ploughing, harrow the field to break up big clumps of soil into something finer. Beans need good contact with the soil to germinate evenly, so a lumpy field means patchy growth. 
### Ridges or Flat Land? ###
 In the north, where rain is lighter and soil drains well, planting flat saves time, labor, and fuel. In the Middle Belt and South, where heavy rain is common, make ridges about 75 cm apart — they carry excess water away from the roots and help prevent rot. 
### Before Weeds Get a Head Start ###
 Spray a pre-emergence herbicide (like Pendimethalin, or a Metolachlor + Prometryn mix) onto damp soil within a day or two of planting, before the seedlings come up. This keeps weeds down for the first month or so.

### Before You Plant ###
 Pick a well-drained, sandy-loam site — beans don't like wet ground. Use good, healthy seed — varieties like Ewa Oloyin, White/Iron beans, or PBR cowpea are popular choices. 
### When to Plant ###
 In the north (Sudan/Sahel Savanna), plant mid-July to mid-August, to match the shorter rains. In the south and Middle Belt, plant later — late August to mid-September — so harvest lands in the dry months of November/December. 
### Spacing and Depth ###
 For upright varieties, leave 75 cm between rows and 20 cm between plants. For spreading varieties, give plants a bit more room — 25–30 cm apart. Plant seeds 2.5 to 5 cm deep, 2 to 3 seeds per hole. Two weeks after germination, thin each hole down to the 2 strongest seedlings. 
### Looking After the Young Crop ###
 Weed 2–3 weeks after planting, then again 5–6 weeks after. Once the leaves cover the ground, the plants keep new weeds down on their own. A little SSP fertilizer at planting helps the roots and pods develop — beans make their own nitrogen, so they don't need much else. Watch out for thrips, aphids, and Maruca pod borer, and spray at budding, flowering, and podding if you're not growing a resistant variety.

Beans are different from crops like maize or cassava because they make their own nitrogen. Feed them the wrong way and you'll actually get a smaller harvest, not a bigger one. 
### Manure ###
 Well-rotted poultry manure or cow dung work best. Never use fresh, wet manure straight on the field — it burns the young roots and brings in weeds and disease. Let it sit and compost for 4 to 6 weeks first. Spread 2 to 5 tonnes per hectare while preparing the land, and work it into the topsoil about 2 weeks before planting. 
### Chemical Fertilizer ###
 A common mistake is piling on Urea or NPK 15-15-15 — too much nitrogen just gives you a leafy plant with very few flowers or pods. What beans really need is phosphorus, which drives root growth, flowering, and pod filling, along with some potassium. Single Super Phosphate (SSP) is the best pick — it gives both phosphorus and sulfur, which improves seed quality. On very worn-out soil, a light dose of NPK 12-12-17 or NPK 20-10-10 can help as a starter. Apply 100–150 kg (2–3 bags) of SSP per hectare at planting. Dig a small groove about 5 cm from the seed row and 5 cm deep, drop the fertilizer in, and cover — never let it touch the seed directly. 
### Extra Boosts ###
 Treating seeds with a Rhizobium inoculant before planting helps them fix more nitrogen on their own, often meaning you can skip nitrogen fertilizer altogether. If plants look pale or weak just before flowering, a light foliar spray of micronutrients can help them hold onto their flowers.

Bean seedlings grow slowly for their first three weeks, so weeds can easily take over and cut your harvest by half or more if you're not careful. The first 2 to 6 weeks after planting matter most — after that, the plants' leaves spread out and shade the ground, keeping new weeds from taking hold. 
### Using Herbicides ###
 At planting: spray a pre-emergence herbicide (Pendimethalin, or Metolachlor + Prometryn) onto damp soil within a day or two, before the seeds sprout. For grass weeds later on: use a selective grass killer like Quizalofop-p-ethyl or Fluazifop-p-butyl. For broadleaf weeds: there aren't many safe options, since beans are broadleaf too — light spot-spraying with Bentazon or hand weeding is usually the way to go. Never spray Glyphosate or Paraquat on a growing bean field — it'll kill the crop along with the weeds. 
### Weeding by Hand ###
 First round: 2 to 3 weeks after planting. Second round: 5 to 6 weeks after planting, done gently so you don't disturb the shallow roots or knock off flowers. Keeping to the 75 cm x 20 cm spacing also helps the plants close ranks faster and shade out weeds.

Growing beans in rotation with other crops keeps the soil healthy, breaks up pest problems, and gets more out of the land over time. Beans leave behind roughly 40–80 kg of nitrogen per hectare for whatever's planted next. Since beans aren't a grain, pests and diseases that live off grain crops can't survive on them. Switching between shallow-rooted grains and deep-rooted beans keeps the soil structure in good shape. 
### A Simple 3-Year Rotation ###
 Northern Savanna: Year 1 maize or sorghum, Year 2 beans, Year 3 millet or groundnuts. Southern and Middle Belt: Year 1 yam or cassava, Year 2 beans, Year 3 maize. 
### Good Habits ###
 Don't plant beans on the same plot two seasons running — it invites soil diseases like Fusarium root rot and lets bean pests build up. After harvest, plough the leftover stalks back into the soil instead of burning them — it adds organic matter for the next crop. If you plant a grain like maize right after beans, you can cut back nitrogen fertilizer by 30–50%, since the soil is already enriched.

Left unchecked, pests can wipe out almost an entire bean harvest in Nigeria. It helps to know which pests show up at which stage of growth. 
### Early On (First 2–4 Weeks) ###
 Cowpea aphids: small black insects that cluster under the leaves, suck the sap, and can spread a virus that curls leaves and stunts growth. Flea beetles: shiny, brownish-yellow beetles that chew holes in young leaves and can spread another damaging virus. 
### Flowering and Podding (the Riskiest Stage) ###
 Legume pod borer (Maruca): the worst pest for beans in Nigeria — caterpillars web up the leaves, flowers, and pods, causing flowers to drop and pods to end up empty. Legume bud thrips: tiny dark insects that attack the flower buds, making them turn brown and fall off before they can open. Pod-sucking bugs: larger brownish bugs that pierce the pods and suck out the nutrients, leaving seeds shriveled, stained, or rotten. 
### In Storage ###
 Cowpea weevil: the main threat once beans are stored — the larvae bore into the seeds and eat them from the inside, leaving small holes and turning good beans into dust.

### Protecting Young Plants ###
 Planting early with the first steady rains gives seedlings a head start over pests. For bad infestations, a systemic insecticide with Imidacloprid, or a Lambda-Cyhalothrin + Imidacloprid mix, works well. For a more natural approach, diluted neem oil or a garlic-chili spray helps keep pests away. 
### Protecting Flowers and Pods ###
 Growing a PBR (pest-resistant) variety naturally fights off Maruca and cuts down how much spraying you need to do. For other varieties, three well-timed sprays work best: one when flower buds first form (around day 30–35) for thrips, one at 50% flowering for Maruca, and one at early podding for pod-sucking bugs. Good chemical choices include Cypermethrin or Lambda-cyhalothrin. 
### Protecting Stored Beans ###
 Skip harsh chemical powders on beans meant for eating — use PICS triple-layer bags instead, which starve weevils of oxygen. You can also spread threshed beans thinly on a dark tarpaulin in strong sun for 4–5 hours — the heat kills weevil eggs and larvae without hurting the seeds. For small amounts at home, mixing in dry pepper, scent leaf, or clean wood ash can help keep weevils away.

Timing matters a lot here — pick too early and the seeds are still small and unripe; wait too long and the pods can split open or get attacked by pests. 
### How to Tell It's Ready ###
 The leaves turn yellow and start falling. The pods change from green to dry brown, tan, or light yellow. The seeds harden and rattle inside the pod when you shake it. 
### Picking the Beans ###
 Most Nigerian farmers pick by hand, gathering the dry pods, or cutting the whole plant at the base if it's ripened evenly. Harvest early in the morning — the dew keeps the pods soft enough that they won't split and spill seed while you're handling them. Sort out any diseased, moldy, or pest-damaged pods as soon as you pick them. 
### Drying After Harvest ###
 Spread the pods out on a clean concrete floor or a tarpaulin and let them dry in the sun for 3 to 5 days, until they're completely brittle — that way they're safe to store or thresh.

Storage is where a lot of harvests get lost in Nigeria — the cowpea weevil can wipe out an entire stock within a few months if it's not protected properly. 
### Threshing and Cleaning ###
 Beat the dried pods gently inside clean sacks to knock the seeds loose, or use a machine thresher for larger amounts. Pour the beans from up high on a windy day, or use a fan, to blow away the dust and broken pod pieces. Pick out any cracked, stony, or pest-damaged beans by hand. 
### Two Ways to Store Safely ###
 
### PICS Triple Bagging ###
 Pour the clean, dry beans into the innermost bag and twist and tie it shut. Seal the second bag over it. Put the whole thing inside the outer woven sack. The insects trapped inside use up the oxygen and die off, keeping the beans safe for over a year without any chemicals. 
### Airtight Bins ###
 Pour dried beans into a plastic or metal drum with a tight screw-top lid. Fill it as close to the top as you can, to leave little room for air. Seal the rim with a rubber gasket or nylon liner before closing the lid tight. 
### A Few Storage Basics ###
 Beans should be below 12% moisture before storing — bite a seed, and it should crack sharply, not feel soft or chewy. Keep bags or drums off the floor on wooden pallets, somewhere cool, dry, well-ventilated, and free of rodents.

Cassava is a starchy root vegetable that grows from a woody shrub native to South America, also known as yuca or manioc. It's a vital calorie source for hundreds of millions of people across tropical regions, largely because it holds up so well against drought. It looks a bit like a long potato, with rough brown skin covering firm white flesh. It's high in carbohydrates and vitamin C, though fairly low in protein. One important safety note: cassava should never be eaten raw, since it contains natural toxins that release cyanide. Proper peeling, soaking, and cooking make it perfectly safe to eat. It's a hugely versatile crop in the kitchen. It gets boiled, mashed, or fried as a side dish, or processed into West African staples like garri and fufu. It's also ground into a naturally gluten-free flour used in baking, and its starch is extracted for tapioca, used in puddings and bubble tea pearls.

Nigeria is now the world's largest producer of cassava, growing nearly 20 percent of global output. What started as an unfamiliar foreign plant became the country's ultimate food security fallback through centuries of migration, colonial influence, and steady agricultural adaptation. Cassava first reached West Africa when Portuguese explorers carried it from South America to the Congo Basin around 1558. It entered coastal southern Nigeria through trade with local kingdoms like the Itsekiri, and via Portuguese-held islands such as São Tomé and Fernando Po. For a long time it stayed a minor crop, since many communities didn't yet know how to safely remove its natural cyanide toxins and were understandably wary of it. The real turning point came in the late 19th century, when formerly enslaved people returning to West Africa from Brazil and the Caribbean brought back the knowledge of how to safely grate, soak, ferment, and fry cassava. That processing method turned a toxic root into garri, a shelf-stable food that transformed the local diet. Farmers quickly noticed how resilient the crop was too, thriving in poor soil, resisting locusts, and staying safely hidden underground even during tribal conflicts. From there, cassava spread from the southern coast into northern Nigeria in the early 1900s along Fulani migration routes, then expanded rapidly across the Middle Belt and northern regions after World War I as colonial administrations promoted it to guard against famine. In the 1970s and 80s, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture in Ibadan developed high-yielding, disease-resistant varieties that cemented Nigeria's place as an agricultural powerhouse. Today, cassava is grown across 24 of Nigeria's 36 states, mostly by smallholder farmers. Beyond feeding millions through fufu and garri, it now feeds into industrial starches, ethanol, animal feed, and high-quality cassava flour aimed at cutting down Nigeria's expensive wheat imports.

Cassava is very much a warm tropical crop, doing best at temperatures between 25 and 29 degrees Celsius. Growth slows noticeably below 15 degrees, and the plant stops growing entirely, or dies, if temperatures drop below 10 degrees or it faces frost. It needs annual rainfall of around 1,000 to 1,500 millimetres, though it can tolerate dry spells and semi-arid conditions down to about 500 millimetres, with the tradeoff being reduced root yield. Full sun matters too, with 10 to 12 hours of direct light a day needed for the best growth. On the soil side, cassava prefers deep, loose, sandy loam or light loamy soils that let the roots expand easily. Good drainage is essential, since wet, heavy clay or waterlogged ground causes the roots to rot and invites pests. A pH between 5.5 and 6.5 is ideal, though it can tolerate acidic soils down to 4.5. Interestingly, cassava can grow in low-fertility soils where other crops struggle, but overly rich soil actually works against it, pushing the plant toward leaf and stem growth instead of building up the tuber roots.

Land preparation starts with clearing away weeds, bushes, and stones from the site, ideally without burning the vegetation, so the organic matter stays in the soil. Primary tillage follows, ploughing 20 to 30 centimetres deep with a tractor or hand tools to break up compacted layers and bury weeds, then harrowing 10 to 14 days later to break large clods down into a fine, loose tilth. From there, the soil gets shaped into ridges or mounds spaced about a metre apart, which prevents waterlogging, improves aeration, and makes harvesting easier down the line. Flat planting only really works on well-drained, loose sandy loam in low-rainfall areas with no waterlogging risk. Ridges are generally the better choice, especially for mechanical farming or fields that see heavy rain, built 30 to 40 centimetres high. Mounds are more common for manual farming or stony soils, built up to about 50 centimetres high with a metre of spacing between them. Right before planting, a pre-emergence herbicide is often applied to keep the field weed-free for the first eight weeks, and well-rotted poultry manure or compost can be worked into the ridges if the soil fertility is on the poor side. It's also worth planning ahead for the dry season: since dried cassava leaves that drop to the ground later on create a real fire hazard, clearing a bare strip about 2 to 3 metres wide around the farm's perimeter acts as a fire belt, helping stop wandering bushfires from reaching the crop.

Since cassava is grown from stem cuttings rather than seeds, choosing healthy parent plants is the single most important step. Stems should come from mature, disease-free plants that are 8 to 18 months old, with thick, strong growth. These get cut into stakes 20 to 30 centimetres long using a sharp knife or cutlass, and each stake needs at least 4 to 6 node buds, the small bumps where new sprouts will emerge. Planting happens at the start of the rainy season, once the soil is consistently moist. Stakes are spaced a metre apart in both directions, roughly 10,000 stands per hectare, and inserted either at a 45-degree angle or straight down. The node buds absolutely must point upward: planting a stem upside down ruins the yield. About two-thirds of each stake goes into the ridge, leaving the top third exposed. A couple of weeks after planting, it's worth walking the farm to check for stakes that failed to sprout or got washed away by rain, replacing them quickly so no field space goes to waste. If a single stake sends up four or five shoots, gently snap off the weakest ones by hand, leaving just two or three strong shoots per stand, so the plant channels its energy into building roots rather than excess leaves. Depending on the variety, the roots are usually ready for harvest 9 to 12 months after planting.

Cassava is especially hungry for potassium, which drives tuber bulking, boosts starch content, and improves drought resistance, making it the single most important nutrient for the crop. Nitrogen supports early stem development and canopy growth during the first three to four months, though too much of it later in the cycle pushes the plant toward lush leaves at the expense of the tubers. Phosphorus matters most in the first few weeks, supporting early root establishment and cell division. Cassava can survive in nutrient-poor soil, but organic manure and mineral fertilizer together can boost tuber yields by more than 30 percent. Poultry manure is the top recommendation, though well-rotted cow dung, compost, or green manure work well too, improving soil structure, helping it hold moisture, and slowly releasing micronutrients. It's typically applied at 5 to 10 tonnes per hectare, or roughly 200 grams per planting hole, worked into the soil one to two weeks before planting so it has time to partially decompose without burning the young cuttings. It can also go on as a top dressing four weeks after planting if it's already fully cured. Mineral fertilizer should only go down when the soil is moist, split into stages to avoid nutrients washing away. From planting through week four, an NPK blend like 15:15:15 or 17:17:17 at around 200 kilograms per hectare gives the roots a strong starter dose. Around month two to three, 100 kilograms per hectare of urea or CAN tops up nitrogen for full canopy development. Then from month four to six, 150 kilograms per hectare of a high-potassium blend like NPK 12:12:17 or Muriate of Potash maximises tuber size and starch buildup. In Nigeria specifically, specialized blends like NPKS 3.5:13:34:4.5 are also widely used to deliver extra potassium and sulfur, paired with a urea top-dressing. Two application methods are common: the ring method, digging a shallow trench about 5 centimetres deep in a circle roughly 20 centimetres from the stem, dropping the fertilizer in, and covering it to stop evaporation or runoff; and the half-moon method, used on sloped land or ridges, where a semi-circular trench is dug on the uphill side of the plant instead. Either way, fertilizer should never touch the stem or cutting directly, since that causes chemical burns that can kill the plant.

The first three to four months are the critical window for weed control, since young cassava plants grow slowly and can't compete for sunlight, water, or nutrients during that stretch. Once the canopy closes around month four, the shade takes over and naturally suppresses further weed growth. Left unchecked during that early window, weeds can cut yields by 40 to 90 percent. Hand weeding is the most common method for smallholders, usually done in three to four rounds at weeks 3, 8, 12, and 16. Planting at a standard 1 by 1 metre spacing, around 10,000 plants per hectare, helps too, since it gets the leaves touching and shading out weeds sooner. Intercropping with fast-growing, low-lying crops like cowpeas, groundnuts, or melons acts as a living mulch that covers bare soil, and cover crops like Mucuna planted during land preparation can smother stubborn weeds before the cassava even goes in. Herbicides are also an option where labor is limited. Pre-emergence herbicides, applied within two to three days of planting before any weeds or cassava buds sprout, keep the field clean for the first 8 to 12 weeks, with common options including Primextra Gold or formulations containing Diuron or Alachlor. From around week eight onward, post-emergence herbicides target weeds that have already grown, using safe grass-killers like Fluazifop-p-butyl or Quizalofop that won't harm the cassava, or broader options like Glufosinate-ammonium or Paraquat for broadleaf weeds where permitted. These broader herbicides are non-selective, so a spray shield or deflector nozzle is essential, kept low to avoid hitting the green cassava stems or leaves, which would stunt or kill the plant. A good integrated approach ties this all together: a pre-emergence herbicide in the first few days, a light spot-weeding or shielded post-emergence spray around weeks 8 to 9, and a final hand weeding around weeks 12 to 14 that doubles as "earthing up," packing loose soil back onto the ridges to protect any exposed roots from sun damage and drying out. After month four, the canopy has closed and no further weeding is usually needed. On smaller farms, mulching the base of the ridges with dried grass or organic debris during the dry season also helps hold onto whatever soil moisture remains.

Cassava is a heavy feeder that stays in the ground for 9 to 18 months, steadily stripping the soil of nutrients, especially potassium and phosphorus. Planting it on the same plot season after season eventually leads to stunted roots and poor yields, so it needs to be rotated with crops that have shorter lifecycles and different root depths to give the soil time to recover. Legumes like cowpea, soybeans, and groundnuts make the best rotation partners, since they pump nitrogen back into the soil while cassava depletes it. Cereals like maize, sorghum, and millet have shallow, fibrous roots that feed on the topsoil, giving the deeper layers cassava relies on a chance to rest. Cover crops like Mucuna or pigeon pea work well during fallow periods too, smothering stubborn weeds like spear grass and adding organic matter once plowed back into the ridges. In the southern and Middle Belt zones, a common four-year cycle runs: cassava planted in the early rains and harvested around 12 months later; then maize intercropped with cowpea in the following wet season, followed by fallow or vegetables like ugu in the dry season; then yam or sweet potato the next wet season, with organic manure worked in over the dry season; before looping back to cassava. It works because maize and yam draw on the topsoil while cowpea fixes nitrogen, so the soil structure has fully recovered by the time cassava returns. In the northern Sudan and Guinea Savannah zones, the cycle looks a little different: cassava using early-maturing varieties, harvested in 9 to 12 months; then soybeans or groundnuts the next wet season, with livestock grazing adding manure over the dry season; then sorghum or millet the following wet season, with the dry season used for land preparation; before looping back to cassava again. Groundnuts and soybeans break up the hard subsoil here and leave nitrogen behind for the next cassava cycle. A few things matter for making rotation actually work: clearing away old woody stumps and diseased leaves after harvest rather than leaving them on the ridges, since they can harbor cassava mosaic virus or whiteflies; flattening and re-ridging the deep holes cassava leaves behind before planting the next, shallower-rooted crop; and when the rotation reaches its legume phase, plowing the green vines and pods back into the soil as green manure and letting them decay for two to three weeks before rebuilding the ridges. Where land is tight, farmers sometimes use a kind of hidden rotation, planting maize and cowpea first and adding cassava stakes four to six weeks later, so the maize and cowpea get harvested in three to four months and leave cassava the field to itself for the rest of its cycle. Beyond restoring soil nutrients, rotation also smothers weeds early, breaks the cycle of pests and diseases that can't survive on non-host crops, and gives farmers a source of quicker cash flow while they wait on the year-long cassava harvest.

Because cassava stays in the ground for close to a year, it's exposed to both insect pests and larger animal pests over that stretch. Whiteflies are tiny, powdery-white insects that sap juice from the underside of leaves, but the bigger concern is that they spread Cassava Mosaic Virus, which curls and yellows the leaves and severely stunts root growth. Cassava green mites bite and suck sap from the top leaves, leaving them speckled, yellowish, and candle-like, while cassava mealybugs cluster on stems like tiny cotton balls and inject toxins that cause "bunchy tops" and shoot dieback; both tend to thrive during the dry season. Variegated grasshoppers, large and brightly colored in yellow, black, and green, show up in large numbers between November and March and can strip leaves and bark right off the stems. Beyond insects, cutting grass, also known as the greater cane rat, and giant rats burrow into the ridges to chew up mature roots, while bush fowls scratch at the soil to expose and peck at younger roots. Wandering cattle, goats, and sheep are another real threat, trampling ridges and eating the green canopy; mature cassava leaves do contain cyanide that can sometimes deter or even poison livestock, but hungry animals will still tear through a farm overnight given the chance.

For whiteflies and the mosaic virus they carry, planting resistant, improved stakes from IITA, such as TMS 98/0505 or TMS 30572, is by far the most effective defense, along with rogueing, uprooting and burning, any plant showing twisted, yellow leaves early before the virus can spread further. Against mites and mealybugs, planting early in the rainy season gives the crop time to mature and toughen up before the dry season pest pressure peaks, and it helps to avoid heavy chemical spraying, since that wipes out the local predatory mites and wasps that naturally keep these pests in check. For grasshoppers, clearing and digging up the farm borders during the dry season exposes their egg pods to sunlight and predators, and spraying an approved insecticide along the borders early in the morning, while the young nymphs are still clustered and slow-moving, is an effective follow-up. Against cutting grass and bush fowl, keeping the farm perimeter completely clear and brushed works well, since these animals avoid open ground that leaves them exposed to hawks and hunters. Wire mesh fencing buried at least 15 centimetres deep is worth the investment on smaller or high-value farms, and traditional wire-loop snares along known animal tracks are another option. For cattle and other livestock, planting dense, thorny live fences like Jatropha curcas or Gliricidia sepium around the farm boundary keeps animals from pushing through, and talking with local leaders and pastoralist groups ahead of planting helps make sure the farm doesn't sit across a traditional grazing or watering route.

Since harvested cassava roots start spoiling within 48 to 72 hours, harvest timing has to be planned right alongside processing plans, not as an afterthought. Most cassava is ready 9 to 12 months after planting, though early-maturing IITA varieties can be ready in as little as 7 to 9 months, and some late varieties can stay in the ground for up to 18. The best window is the rainy season or early dry season, since rain softens the soil and makes it far easier to pull the roots without snapping them. Look for yellowing and shedding of the lower leaves, along with cracking in the soil around the base as the swelling roots push upward, as the clearest signs the crop is ready. Most Nigerian smallholders harvest by hand. It starts with clearing the canopy, cutting the stems down with a cutlass and leaving a stump of about 30 to 50 centimetres, then bundling the cut stems and storing them upright in the shade to reuse as planting stakes next season. If the ground is hard, the soil around the base gets loosened with a hoe or digging fork, carefully, so as not to slice into the tubers underground, since wounded roots rot even faster. The stump is then held firmly with both hands and pulled up and slightly forward, feet planted wide, to lift the whole tuber cluster out of the ridge, with a wooden stick used as a lever for stubborn roots. Each tuber is then chopped away from the central base with a cutlass, leaving a small one to two centimetre stub of stalk attached, since cutting too close to the flesh exposes the core and speeds up spoilage. Once out of the ground, bruised or cut roots get sorted away from the undamaged ones and processed or eaten first, since they spoil fastest. The harvested roots are moved into shade or covered with cassava leaves to protect them from direct sun, and then transported quickly to a frying shed or local mill, since in Nigeria most of the harvest goes straight into making garri, fufu, or lafun.

Fresh cassava roots spoil fast, within 48 to 72 hours, due to rapid deterioration after harvest, so storage really means choosing the right method quickly rather than delaying a decision. Leaving mature roots unharvested in the ground keeps them fresh for up to a year, though they can turn woody over time. Burying roots in layers of moist straw, soil, or sawdust, sometimes called mound or pit storage, keeps them fresh for four to eight weeks by holding humidity steady without waterlogging them. Sealed polyethylene bags preserve freshness for two to three weeks, while peeling and freezing the roots extends shelf life up to a year, and raw whole roots last about two weeks under basic refrigeration. Processing opens up longer storage options. Chipping the roots and sun-drying them below 12 percent moisture allows bag storage for six months to a year. Turning roots into flour or starch produces a dry powder that keeps for over a year in airtight containers. And frying and fermenting grated cassava into garri creates a genuinely shelf-stable staple that stores safely for one to two years as long as it's kept dry. A few things matter no matter which method is chosen. Physical damage, like broken tips or cuts in the skin, speeds up spoilage dramatically, triggering browning and rot within hours, so gentle handling is essential throughout. High humidity helps whole roots hold onto their moisture, but too much wetness invites fungal mold, and stored fresh roots need enough airflow to stop heat from building up, since trapped heat speeds up decay.

In Nigeria, rice is far more than a grain on the plate. It's the country's most critical staple and food security crop, eaten daily in nearly every household, and it carries real weight as an economic driver, a centerpiece at celebrations, and a constant focus of national agricultural policy. Globally, most rice traded and eaten is Asian rice, Oryza sativa, but Nigeria has a special place in rice history as one of the native homes of African rice, Oryza glaberrima. These days, most Nigerian farmers grow improved, high-yielding varieties like FARO 44 and FARO 52, bred specifically to perform well in local growing conditions. The crop is cultivated across a mix of ecosystems: the majority comes from lowland and Fadama swamp areas that rely on seasonal flooding, a good share comes from upland, rain-fed farming on hillsides, and a smaller portion is grown on fully irrigated modern farms. Nigerian consumers tend to group rice into a few broad categories. Local unpolished rice, like Ofada rice from Ogun State or Abakaliki rice from Ebonyi, is short-grained, parboiled only briefly, and deliberately left unpolished, which gives it a strong, distinctive aroma and keeps more nutrients from the bran intact. Local commercial milled rice is the clean, stone-free white long-grain rice processed in modern Nigerian mills under brands like Mama Gold, Big Bull, and Ga'ate, produced at major hubs including Kebbi, Kano, Kaduna, Niger, Taraba, and Benue. Then there's imported or foreign rice, typically highly polished, parboiled long-grain rice historically brought in from Thailand or India, though border closures and foreign exchange restrictions have pushed domestic brands to take over most of that market share. Rice also sits at the heart of Nigerian food culture. It's the base for iconic dishes like Jollof rice, fried rice, coconut rice, and Tuwon Shinkafa, a northern rice swallow made from broken grains, and no Owanbe party, wedding, Eid celebration, or Christmas gathering feels complete without large catering pots of parboiled long-grain rice. Because it matters so much day to day, the price of a standard 50kg bag of rice has become a widely used, informal gauge that everyday Nigerians rely on to judge inflation and the cost of living. And since the country spends significant foreign currency importing food, the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and the Central Bank of Nigeria keep rolling out credit initiatives to support local millers and smallholder farmers, all aimed at pushing Nigeria toward complete self-sufficiency in rice.

Rice farming in Nigeria goes back thousands of years. Long before modern varieties arrived, farmers across West African floodplains and savannah zones were already cultivating Oryza glaberrima, the indigenous African rice, and this had been going on for well over 3,500 years. Early communities, including Yoruba and Hausa farmers, grew and traded local rice varieties as part of regional commerce. Things began to change around 1890, when the higher-yielding Asian rice, Oryza sativa, was introduced into the forest zones of western Nigeria. Over the following decades it steadily took over from the native species, and by 1960 it had largely replaced it in most farming areas. A major turning point came in the early 1940s, when commercial swamp rice farming took hold in Abakaliki in eastern Nigeria, quickly becoming a key economic activity in the region. However, from the late 1960s through the 1990s, local production couldn't keep pace with the growing appetite of Nigeria's cities, and the country became heavily dependent on imported milled rice despite having plenty of farmland to work with. Recent decades have brought renewed momentum. The Agricultural Transformation Agenda, launched in 2011, drew in private investment and helped grow the number of modern integrated rice mills from just a handful of small operators to dozens of large commercial facilities. Then in 2015, border closures, import tariffs, and support schemes like the Anchor Borrowers' Program pushed local production even higher as part of a broader self-sufficiency drive. Today Nigeria produces millions of metric tons of rice each year, though farmers still contend with high input costs, limited mechanization, and flood management challenges.

Rice is a warm-season crop that wants a hot, humid climate to really thrive. It grows best with average temperatures between 21 and 37 degrees Celsius, and while it can tolerate spikes up to around 40 degrees, cool nights or unexpected cold snaps hurt both growth and grain filling. Bright, sunny days matter a lot too, especially during the ripening period in the final 30 to 45 days before harvest, since that's when proper grain development depends on it. Water is non-negotiable for rice. The crop needs a dependable water source or heavy rainfall totaling at least 1,000 millimetres over the growing season. Lowland rice fields need regular flooding, kept at around 2 to 4 inches of standing water, while upland rice gets by on steady rainfall or soil moisture without needing deep flooding. On the soil side, clay, clay loam, and silt loam soils work best because they hold water well and resist draining too quickly. A slightly acidic to neutral pH, somewhere between 5.0 and 7.5, suits rice well. Lowland fields need soil that can be puddled into a dense, water-holding layer, while upland rice does better in looser, well-drained soil that doesn't fully waterlog. Because rice draws heavily on nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, rich organic matter or added fertilizer is essential to keep up with its appetite.

Getting the land ready starts with site selection: a lowland Fadama area or an upland plot with good water retention and fertile clay-loam or clayey soil works best. From there, the land gets cleared of trees, stumps, shrubs, and dense weeds, using cutlasses and hoes on smaller farms or bulldozers on larger ones, and the cleared debris is either packed away or burned so weed roots are exposed to the sun. Tillage comes next: the soil is plowed with a hoe, an animal-drawn ridger, or a tractor plow to bury weeds and break up compacted ground, then harrowed to break large clods into finer particles. For lowland fields, this is followed by puddling, flooding the field and churning the wet soil into mud, which suppresses weeds and cuts down on water seeping away too quickly. The field is then leveled to create a smooth, even surface, since uniform water depth across the plot helps prevent both weed growth and uneven crop development. Finally, small mud bunds or ridges are built around the plot boundaries to trap and hold the standing water that lowland rice depends on.

Getting rice planting right in Nigeria starts with choosing good seed, such as FARO 44 or NERICA, and preparing the right kind of soil, ideally a clayey or loamy type found in river valleys and Fadama areas that can hold water well. Timing matters a lot. Farmers typically clear their land between November and February, then wait for the rains to settle in before planting, usually in May or June, or as late as July in areas prone to flooding. Once the land is cleared, it's ploughed and harrowed to leave a smooth, weed-free bed ready for planting. There are two common ways to get the rice into the ground. Some farmers raise seedlings in a small shaded nursery for about three weeks before transplanting the healthy ones into the flooded main field, spacing them about 20 by 20 centimetres apart. Others plant directly, sowing two to three seeds into holes or drilled rows roughly 2 to 4 centimetres deep in wet soil. Once the crop is in the ground, ongoing care makes a big difference. Weeds need to be cleared by hand, usually around two to three weeks after sprouting and again at six to seven weeks. Fertilizer helps too: NPK is applied early on, with urea following around 30 to 45 days later to push yields higher. Throughout it all, the lowland fields need to stay properly irrigated or waterlogged, since rice depends on plenty of moisture to grow well.

The best rice yields in Nigeria come from combining basal organic manure, which builds up soil structure, with a split application of inorganic NPK and urea fertilizer timed to the crop's growth stages, especially with common varieties like FARO 44. Organic manure needs to be fully decomposed and dried before it goes into the field, since fresh manure can generate harmful microbial heat and even trigger pest outbreaks like stem borers. Poultry manure tends to give the best yield returns in Nigeria, though cow dung and green manure legumes like Sesbania work well too. It's spread evenly across the field two to three weeks before planting and worked thoroughly into the soil during plowing or bed preparation, typically at a rate of 5 to 10 tonnes per hectare depending on how depleted the soil is. Rice is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and a golden rule worth remembering is to never mix NPK and urea in the first application, since NPK blends already carry enough nitrogen for the early stage. The full fertilizer schedule follows the crop's growth: at planting, or within the first two weeks after transplanting, about four bags (200 kg) per hectare of an NPK blend like 15:15:15, 20:10:10, or 27:13:13 gets broadcast evenly with the field holding 2 to 3 centimetres of water. Three to four weeks after sowing, during active tillering, one to one and a half bags (50 to 75 kg) per hectare of urea goes down after weeding, with the soil kept moist but not deeply flooded to avoid the fertilizer leaching away. Then six to eight weeks after sowing, as the seed heads start forming, one more bag (50 kg) per hectare of urea, along with optional potassium, is broadcast into the stands to support grain size and panicle development. A few rules make a real difference here. Always drop the water level to 2 to 3 centimetres before broadcasting any fertilizer, since too much water washes it away or lets it leach too deep for the roots to reach. Always weed the field before applying urea, otherwise the weeds soak up the nitrogen before the rice gets a chance to use it. And never apply urea during or after flowering, since excess nitrogen at that stage makes the plant grow too heavy, causes it to fall over, and can delay the grain from maturing properly.

Weeds are a serious threat to rice, capable of cutting yields by up to 80 percent if left unchecked, since they compete hard for sunlight, water, and nutrients. Managing them well takes an integrated approach: solid land preparation, careful water management, hand-pulling, and targeted herbicide use working together. On the cultural and mechanical side, the stale seedbed technique works well: flooding the field two weeks before planting forces weed seeds to germinate early, and they're then plowed under or sprayed with a non-selective herbicide before the rice goes in. Once the crop is transplanted, keeping a steady water level of 5 to 10 centimetres in lowland paddies helps too, since most upland weeds simply can't germinate or survive underwater. Manual weeding rounds this out, with a first hand-pulling or hoeing session two to three weeks after sowing or transplanting, and a second one at five to six weeks, always done before applying urea. Herbicides add another layer of control, chosen carefully based on whether the rice is upland or lowland and always applied when the soil is moist. In the first few days after sowing or transplanting, a pre-emergence, broad-spectrum barrier herbicide such as pretilachlor, oxadiazon, or butachlor stops grass and broadleaf seeds from sprouting in the first place. About 10 to 14 days after planting, an early post-emergence, selective contact herbicide like propanil combined with triclopyr, or bispyribac-sodium, kills young, actively growing grasses and sedges without harming the rice itself. Then three to four weeks after planting, a late post-emergence, selective systemic herbicide such as 2,4-D amine or metsulfuron-methyl targets the stubborn broadleaf weeds and heavier sedges that are still hanging on. A few spraying guidelines help these herbicides actually work. Sprayer nozzles need to be checked for leaks and fitted with a flood-jet or flat-fan nozzle for even coverage. When spraying a post-emergence herbicide in a lowland field, the water should be drained first so the weed leaves are fully exposed to the chemical, then the field is re-flooded about 48 hours later to lock in the control. And as with any chemical application, protective gear like gloves, a mask, and boots should be worn, with spraying done in the same direction as the wind to avoid breathing in any drift.

Rice does best when it isn't planted on the same field season after season. Continuous rice farming drains nitrogen from the soil, lets weeds like wild rice or Striga take hold, and gives soil-borne pests such as stem borers room to multiply year after year. Rotating rice with other crops breaks that cycle in several ways: legumes replenish soil nitrogen and cut down on fertilizer costs, switching crops interrupts the life cycles of rice-specific pests and diseases, alternating between flooded and dryland conditions helps control both aquatic and terrestrial weeds, and deep-rooted dryland crops help break up compacted soil left behind by rice farming. Nigerian farmers use a few common rotation patterns depending on their zone. Rotating rice with cowpea or soybeans works well nationwide, since the legumes fix nitrogen and break the stem borer cycle while also producing a valuable secondary crop. In irrigated lowlands and Fadama areas, farmers often follow rice with dry-season vegetables like tomato, okra, or pepper, taking advantage of residual soil moisture for extra income. In the Middle Belt and northern Nigeria, sesame or groundnut is a popular follow-up crop, thriving on lighter residual moisture while lowering nematode pressure. On degrading lowland soils, farmers sometimes plant green manure crops like Mucuna or Sesbania and plough them back into the soil to rebuild organic matter before the next rainy season.

Rice in Nigeria faces pressure from insect pests, vertebrate pests, and diseases at nearly every growth stage. Among insects, stem borers are considered the most destructive, with larvae boring into the stem to cause "dead hearts" in young plants or "white heads" at flowering. The African rice gall midge is especially active in lowland and irrigated systems, forming tube-like "silver shoot" galls that stop panicles from developing. Stalk-eyed flies cause similar damage by burrowing into young shoots, while rice bugs and stink bugs attack developing grain during the milky stage, leaving kernels empty, discolored, or malformed. Armyworms and leaf folders round out the list, feeding on or folding leaves in ways that cut down photosynthesis. Beyond insects, quelea birds can strip fields of grain during ripening, especially in the north and central regions, while rats and cane rats cut down mature tillers overnight to feed on the sweet stems and panicles. Root-knot nematodes are a quieter threat, attacking root systems underground and causing stunted, yellowing plants in upland soils.

Managing these pests works best with a mix of tactics. Planting early at the start of the rains and choosing resistant varieties like FARO 44 or NERICA helps guard against stem borers and gall midge, with systemic insecticides such as carbofuran or fipronil kept in reserve for when damage crosses an economic threshold. Keeping field borders free of wild grasses reduces grain-sucking bugs, and targeted spraying in the early morning or late afternoon, when the bugs are active, helps too. Coordinating planting dates with neighboring farmers and using scaring devices or netting in the final weeks before harvest can cut bird losses, while clearing brush, destroying burrows, and setting perimeter traps helps keep rodents in check. When it comes to chemical control, products applied at the correct dosage are formulated to target the pest without harming the rice plant itself. Chlorantraniliprole (sold as Rynaxypyr or Ferterra) targets stem borers by acting on their muscle receptors, applied as granules 25 to 30 days after transplanting or as a foliar spray. Fipronil, used against both gall midge and stem borers, is absorbed systemically through the roots or stem, applied either as soil granules early on or as a foliar spray once pests are detected. Cartap hydrochloride, sold as Padan, also targets stem borers, stopping their feeding quickly while remaining low in toxicity to the rice plant itself. For farmers who prefer to avoid chemicals entirely, botanical and biological options carry no risk of harming the crop. Neem seed kernel extract or azadirachtin spray acts as a natural anti-feedant, stopping pests from feeding within hours. Neem oil mixed with a little soap repels stalk-eyed flies and stem borer moths from laying eggs. Trichogramma japonicum, a tiny parasitic wasp, can also be released to destroy stem borer eggs before the larvae ever get a chance to bore into the stem. Even safe products can stress the crop if mishandled, so a few precautions matter: stick closely to label dosages, since overdosing or stacking chemicals can scorch leaf tips; spray early in the morning or late afternoon rather than in the heat of the day, which can worsen leaf scorch; and avoid broad spraying during flowering, since this can disrupt pollination.

Rice is usually ready for harvest three to four months after planting, often between October and December for crops grown in the rainy season. The clearest sign it's ready is when 80 to 85 percent of the panicles have turned golden-yellow, brown, or straw-colored. About two weeks before cutting, farmers drain the water from lowland paddy fields so the soil firms up enough to support workers and equipment. When it's time to cut the rice, smallholders typically use a sharp hand sickle to slice the stalks about 10 to 15 centimetres above the ground, while larger commercial farms rely on combine harvesters that cut, thresh, and clean the grain all in one pass over flat fields. After cutting, the grain still needs to be separated and dried. Manual threshing involves beating the cut bundles against a hard wooden board or a clean concrete floor to knock the grains loose, and winnowing follows by letting the wind or a fan blow away the empty husks and chaff. The clean paddy is then spread out under the sun on tarpaulins for a day or two until it's dried down to a safe moisture level of about 12 to 14 percent, which keeps mold and spoilage at bay before milling or bagging.

Good rice storage comes down to keeping grain moisture between 12 and 14 percent, since that's what prevents mold, insect infestation, and spoilage from taking hold. Poor storage practices are behind a significant share of Nigeria's post-harvest losses, and whether the grain is unhulled paddy or milled white rice, a few conditions have to be met to protect its quality and market value. It starts with thorough drying right after threshing, whether in the sun or by machine. Paddy needs to come down to 12 to 14 percent moisture, while milled rice needs to go a bit lower, to 10 to 12 percent, since wet grain causes internal heating and rot. Cleaning and winnowing come next, removing chaff, stones, straw, and broken kernels before bagging, since leftover debris traps moisture and draws insects. Before any bags go into storage, the warehouse itself should be cleaned and treated with approved food-safe insecticides or fumigants to clear out any resident weevils or moths. There are a few common ways to actually store the grain. Modern hermetic bags, like PICS bags or ZeroFly Combi bags, use multiple layers of airtight plastic sealing that cut off oxygen inside the bag, suffocating insect pests and weevil larvae without needing any chemicals. Standard polypropylene or jute sacks are more traditional, packed and stacked neatly inside a concrete warehouse, though the bags should never touch the floor or walls directly, since moisture can seep out of concrete into the rice, so stacking on wooden pallets is important. Larger commercial millers and national grain reserves often use metal or concrete silos instead, which come with automated temperature sensors and aeration fans that blow cool air uniformly through thousands of tonnes of grain. A few extra precautions round out good storage. Leaving at least a metre of space between bag stacks and the warehouse walls allows for proper inspection and airflow, while sealing cracks, drainage areas, and gaps under doors with metal wire mesh keeps rats and mice fully locked out. For smaller-scale home storage, mixing in dry bay leaves or cloves works as a genuinely effective, natural insect repellent.

Yam is a starchy edible tuber that grows underground from a tropical climbing vine in the Dioscorea family. It has a rough, bark-like skin, usually dark brown, and a dense, neutral-tasting flesh that can be white, off-white, yellow, or purple depending on the variety. It's a major food staple across West Africa, the Caribbean, and parts of Asia. People often mix yam up with sweet potato, but they're not related at all. True yams belong to the Dioscoreaceae family, can grow quite large, sometimes over 50 pounds, and need to be peeled because of their rough skin. Sweet potatoes belong to a completely different family, have smooth skin, and taste noticeably sweeter and moister. In North America, sweet potatoes are frequently mislabeled as yams, which is where a lot of the confusion comes from. In the kitchen, yam is typically boiled or fried and eaten in chunks alongside stews, or boiled and pounded into a smooth, dough-like consistency to make pounded yam, which is eaten with soup. Purple varieties, sometimes called ube, are also popular in desserts and pastries, especially in parts of Asia.

Yam has been grown in Nigeria for more than 5,000 years, tracing back to wild forest roots gathered by indigenous West African peoples long before recorded history. Independent domestication is believed to have taken hold somewhere between 5000 and 3000 BCE. Nigeria sits right in the middle of what's known as Africa's Yam Belt, a stretch running from West to Central Africa where the warm, humid climate and clear wet and dry seasons suit the crop well. The crop carries deep cultural weight too. In Yoruba tradition, Ile-Ife is regarded as a cradle of yam history, where early figures like Oreluere are said to have planted the first cultivated yams at Ita Olopo. Among groups like the Igbo, Tiv, Yoruba, and Ebira, yam has long stood for wealth, prestige, and hard work, so much so that a family's status in many farming communities was historically judged by the size of their yam barn. New Yam Festivals, like the Igbo Iri Ji or Iwa Ji, mark the end of the harvest season and give thanks to deities and ancestors before anyone eats from the new crop. Nigeria remains the undisputed global leader in yam production today, growing an estimated 65 to 70 percent of the world's supply, with major output coming from the middle belt and southern states including Taraba, Benue, Niger, Kwara, and Oyo. Pounded yam, known as Iyan, along with boiled, fried, or roasted preparations, keeps the crop central to Nigerian food security and identity.

Yam is a tropical crop through and through, and it does best with plenty of warmth, steady moisture, and a fairly long growing season. Temperatures between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius suit it well; very low temperatures slow growth down, while high heat combined with drought can hurt tuber development. Moisture matters a lot too, especially during the early and middle stages of growth. Somewhere around 1,000 to 1,500 millimetres of well-spread rainfall over the growing season generally works well, though the exact need shifts depending on the variety and location. Too little rain leaves vines weak and tubers small, while too much rain or standing water encourages rot and disease. Good sunlight is essential as well, since shading from trees or taller crops can hold back both vine and tuber growth. On the soil side, yam wants deep, loose, fertile, well-drained ground, ideally loamy or sandy-loam, since that lets the tubers expand freely as they grow. Rich organic matter helps with fertility, moisture retention, and overall soil structure, and because the tubers grow well below the surface, the soil needs to be deep enough to accommodate that. A pH between about 5.5 and 7.0 is generally suitable. Heavy clay soils make both tuber development and harvesting difficult, and waterlogged spots should be avoided altogether. Before planting, it's worth walking the field and, where possible, running a soil test to catch any nutrient gaps early.

Since yam produces its main harvest underground, getting the land ready properly makes a real difference. Start by choosing land with good drainage, no recent history of yam diseases or nematodes, plenty of sunlight, deep soil, and reasonable fertility, while steering clear of anything that stays flooded after rain. Clearing comes next: remove bushes, unwanted vegetation, large roots, stumps, and any crop residue that might be carrying pests or disease, though well-decomposed organic material can still be worked back into the soil afterward. The soil itself needs to be loosened deeply enough for the tuber to develop without obstruction, since compacted ground tends to produce small, misshapen tubers that are harder to harvest without damage. Yam is typically grown on mounds or ridges, particularly where drainage matters. A good mound should be large enough for the tuber to expand into, made of loose soil, able to shed excess water, and ideally enriched with organic matter. Mound height usually runs between 60 and 100 centimetres, spaced about a metre apart, though exact sizing depends on the variety, soil type, and local farming practices. Well-decomposed manure or compost can be worked in during this stage, but fresh, undecomposed manure should never sit directly against the seed yam, since it can invite pests, disease, and excess heat as it breaks down. On sloping land, it's worth taking extra care against erosion: planting across the slope, keeping some vegetation cover, using ridges suited to the terrain, and avoiding stripping all the ground bare all help keep valuable topsoil and nutrients from washing away.

In Nigeria, yam planting usually gets underway between February and April, timed around when the rains settle into your area. Look for a sunny spot with loose, well-drained soil, ideally sandy loam or alluvial soil, and steer clear of heavy clay, which waterlogs easily and rots the tubers. For seed yams, use healthy, disease-free sets weighing roughly 200 to 500 grams. If you're cutting larger tubers into pieces, let the cut slices cure in the shade for two to three days, then rub wood ash or a fungicide onto the cut surfaces to guard against fungal infection before planting. To plant, dig a hole about 15 to 20 centimetres deep at the top of the mound, place the cut surface facing up and the skin facing down, then fill the hole with loose soil and pat it gently. A layer of dry leaves or grass mulched over the mound helps hold in moisture and keep the soil cool. Once the vine sprouts, insert sturdy wooden stakes, roughly two to three metres tall, near the plant and gently train the young vine clockwise around them so it gets the most sunlight. Keep weeds cleared regularly, especially through the first three months, and pay attention to soil moisture without letting water pool. The tubers are typically dug up six to ten months later, once the leaves turn yellow and begin to dry.

Yam needs a good supply of nutrients to support both its vines and its developing tubers, and the three big ones are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Nitrogen drives leaf and vine growth, but too much of it can push the plant toward heavy vine growth at the expense of the tubers themselves. Phosphorus supports root development, helps the plant establish early on, and plays a role in energy transfer. Potassium is especially important for tuber development, moving water and nutrients through the plant, and building overall plant strength and stress tolerance. Organic manure, whether from animals, compost, or decomposed crop residue, brings benefits beyond just nutrients: it improves soil structure, helps the ground hold water, supports microbial activity, and makes nutrients more available to the plant. That said, fertilizer shouldn't be applied blindly. What a field actually needs depends on soil fertility, the yam variety, the previous crop grown there, expected yield, local climate, and the overall farming system. A soil test is the best way to know for sure, and where that's not possible, following guidance from local agricultural extension services beats guessing. It's worth remembering that more fertilizer doesn't mean more yam. Overdoing it wastes money, throws off the nutrient balance, pushes excessive vine growth instead of tuber growth, can damage the plant if misapplied, and adds to environmental pollution. Fertilizer works best applied at the recommended rate and at the right stage of the plant's growth.

Weeds compete hardest with young yam plants during the first three months after planting, so early and regular weeding, done by hand or with light hoeing, makes a real difference in how well the crop establishes itself. Mulching helps here too. Covering the mounds or ridges with dry grass or straw keeps the soil cool, holds in moisture, and suppresses weed growth at the same time, cutting down on how much manual weeding is needed as the season goes on.

Because yam draws heavily on soil fertility and organic matter, it's traditionally grown as the first crop after land is cleared or comes out of fallow. Rotating it with other crops afterward stops soil pests like nematodes and yam beetles from building up, prevents fungal and bacterial tuber rot from lingering in the soil, restores nutrients like nitrogen, and improves overall soil structure while reducing erosion. A common four-year cycle looks like this: in year one, yam goes into rich mounds or ridges at the start of the rainy season between March and May, drawing heavily on potassium and organic nutrients. Year two brings in legumes like cowpea, groundnut, soybeans, or a cover crop like Mucuna, which fix nitrogen back into the soil and interrupt yam's disease cycle. Year three moves to a cereal like maize or sorghum, which makes use of the nitrogen the legumes left behind and brings a different root structure and pest profile into the mix. Year four is left fallow, or planted with a light, shallow-rooted cover crop, giving the soil time to rebuild its organic matter before yam returns to that plot. A couple of things to avoid: don't follow yam with cassava or sweet potato, since they share similar root-rot diseases, pests, and nutrient demands, and avoid planting root crops back-to-back on the same land in general.

Yam tuber beetles are among the most damaging pests, boring deep holes into the underground tubers, which cuts into yield and opens the door for rot to set in. The yam nematode causes dry rot, leading to cracking and dark patches on tubers both in the field and later in storage. Yam scales feed on stored tubers, roughening the skin and drying the yam out over time. Storage beetles and weevils go after whole stored yams and dried yam chips, sometimes known as elubo, reducing them to powdery waste if left unchecked.

Crop rotation with non-host crops and clearing farm debris helps break pest life cycles before they take hold. Planting early in the season, ahead of when beetle populations peak in riverine and savanna zones, also cuts down on damage, as does starting with clean, disease-free planting material. Before planting, seed yams can be treated with hot water, around 50 to 55 degrees Celsius for about 40 minutes, or dipped in an approved fungicidal or insecticidal slurry. Once yams are in storage, coating tubers with wood ash or applying a recommended storage insecticide, such as Thiabendazole, helps guard against scale insects and fungal rot taking hold.

Yam is generally ready for harvest somewhere between six and twelve months after planting, depending on the variety, and the clearest sign is the upper vine leaves turning yellow and starting to wither. Farmers soften the soil around the mound first, then use a spade, hoe, or pointed stick to carefully lift the tubers out without cutting or bruising them, since damaged tubers spoil faster in storage. Some farmers use a technique called milking, doing a first partial harvest at five to six months by cutting away a portion of the main tuber and covering the roots back up, letting smaller seed yams regrow from what's left. After digging, tubers are cleaned of heavy dirt and left to dry or cure in a shaded, well-aired spot for a few hours to a few days, then sorted by size before heading to storage or market.

Good storage starts with careful handling right after harvest: tubers shouldn't be thrown or dropped, badly damaged or diseased ones shouldn't be mixed in with healthy stock, and any surface wounds should be given time to dry and heal before long-term storage begins. Cuts and bruises create easy entry points for the organisms that cause rot, so gentle handling matters throughout. Stored yams need a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot, shielded from direct sunlight, rain, and rodents or other pests. Good airflow is especially important, since trapped moisture is what really encourages rotting. Many farmers in West Africa rely on yam barns for this, structures that keep tubers off the ground, allow air to circulate, provide shade, protect against rain and rodents, and make regular inspection easy without overcrowding the tubers. Checking stored yams regularly for soft spots, rot, mould, insect or rodent damage, and excessive sprouting makes it possible to catch problems early and remove affected tubers before they spread to healthy ones nearby. Most storage losses trace back to a handful of causes: mechanical damage from cuts and bruises during harvest and transport, rot from wounds and unsuitable moisture, rodents and insects feeding on stored tubers, poor ventilation raising humidity, and excessive heat speeding up deterioration and sprouting. A strong harvest can still turn into a real financial loss if storage is treated as an afterthought.

Maize, also called corn, is a tall cereal grain that was first grown by people in Mexico thousands of years ago. It grows on leafy stalks that produce ears full of starchy kernels, and it's one of the most important food crops in the world, feeding both people and livestock. In Nigeria, maize is more than just a crop — it's daily food, a way to earn money, and a source of pride for farmers across the country. It's the crop Nigerians eat the most of, and it links small family farms to big agricultural businesses. What maize means to a farmer shifts depending on the season and where they're farming: For food: maize is eaten fresh or turned into everyday staples like Ogi (a fermented pudding often used for breakfast or weaning babies) and Tuwo Masara (a dense swallow food popular in the north). Roasted or boiled green cobs are also a common roadside snack. For income: farmers sell maize as human food, but they can also sell in bulk to the poultry industry, which relies heavily on it for animal feed, or to mills that turn it into flour, starch, and cereal. By region: farmers in the south plant early with the first rains around March/April, sometimes fitting in a second planting around August. Farmers in the north plant a bit later, between May and July, and northern states now grow the most maize thanks to more sunshine. Some farmers with access to irrigation even grow an off-season crop between October and March, when prices are higher. Growing maize in Nigeria isn't without risk — farmers have to watch out for the Fall Armyworm, which can destroy a field in days, the parasitic weed Striga in the north, and unpredictable rain. That's part of why many farmers now choose drought-tolerant hybrid seeds like the SAMMAZ varieties.

Maize isn't native to Nigeria — it arrived through trade centuries ago and slowly grew into the country's most widely grown cereal, even though it played second fiddle to crops like yam, sorghum, and millet for a long time. 
### How Maize Arrived ###
 Portuguese traders brought maize seeds to the coast around the Bight of Benin and the Niger Delta in the 1500s, originally to feed ships docked at trading posts. Farmers in the south picked it up quickly because it grew fast — about three months — and gave a good yield. Even the Yoruba word for maize, Agbado, hints at this — it roughly translates to "grain of the shores," a nod to where it first landed. 
### A Backyard Crop for Centuries ###
 For nearly 400 years, maize stayed a small backyard crop, mostly in the humid south where there was enough steady moisture for it to grow. Families grew just a little, roasted or boiled fresh, to bridge the gap between harvests when stored yams ran low. The north largely ignored it, sticking with drought-tolerant staples like sorghum and millet. 
### A Crisis That Changed Everything ###
 In 1950, a fungus called American Corn Rust swept through West Africa. Nigeria's local maize varieties had no resistance, and the disease wiped out fields and threatened food supplies. That crisis pushed the government to start taking food crops seriously, not just export crops like cocoa and palm oil, and by 1956 breeding programs had begun in Ibadan to develop rust-resistant seeds. 
### The Push North ###
 After the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) was set up in Ibadan in 1967, things moved fast. By 1983, Nigeria had released its first high-yielding hybrid maize seeds, and researchers bred varieties that could handle drought and resist Striga. That opened up the north to maize farming, and with more sunlight and open land, northern states like Kaduna, Niger, and Katsina overtook the south as Nigeria's main maize-growing region. 
### Where Things Stand Today ###
 Maize overtook sorghum in 2011 to become Nigeria's most widely grown cereal. Nigeria now grows more maize than any other country in Sub-Saharan Africa, but demand from mills, breweries, and feed companies is still higher than what farmers can supply, so the country keeps working to close that gap.

### Climate ###
 Maize needs 600 mm to 1,200 mm of rain spread fairly evenly across a 90 to 120-day growing period. Water matters most around weeks 6 to 8, when the plant is tasseling, flowering, and forming silk. A dry spell at this point can mean empty cobs with no kernels. The best temperatures are 24°C to 30°C. Below 18°C slows germination, and above 35°C during flowering can dry out the pollen and ruin the harvest. Maize needs 6 to 8 hours of strong direct sun a day. This is a big reason northern Nigeria gets higher yields than the humid south — less cloud cover means more sunlight for the plant to use. 
### Soil ###
 Deep, well-drained loam, sandy loam, or silty loam works best — it holds enough moisture without trapping excess water. Maize really doesn't handle standing water. If water sits on the field for more than a day or two, the roots suffocate, leaves turn yellow, and growth stops. Avoid heavy clay that holds water. Ideal soil pH is 5.5 to 7.0. In parts of the south where soil tends to be quite acidic, applying agricultural lime during land prep helps release nutrients like phosphorus that would otherwise be locked up. Soil rich in organic matter holds onto fertilizer better, so it doesn't wash away during heavy rain. The Northern Guinea Savanna — states like Kaduna and Niger — is Nigeria's main maize belt today, thanks to strong sunlight and a clear wet-to-dry season transition.

Good land preparation sets up everything that follows — skip it, and you end up with compacted soil, poor seed contact, and weeds getting the upper hand before your maize even sprouts. 
### Clearing ###
 Clear trees, stumps, and shrubs, especially if you're using a tractor, since buried roots can damage plough discs. Avoid slash-and-burn — burning destroys the organic matter and microbes in the topsoil. It's better to slash the vegetation and let it dry as mulch, or plough it back in to rot. 
### Ploughing ###
 Plough soon after the first rain or two, once the soil is damp but not waterlogged, turning over the top 15 to 20 cm. This buries weeds, breaks up compacted soil, and exposes pests like white grubs to the sun and birds. 
### Harrowing ###
 About 7 to 10 days after ploughing, harrow the field to break big clumps into a fine, crumbly texture. Maize seeds need loose soil to germinate evenly — in cloddy or rocky ground, seeds fall into air pockets and dry out. 
### Building Ridges ###
 Ridges are worth the effort in most parts of Nigeria — maize roots hate standing water, and ridges keep them elevated and well-drained, while also making weeding and fertilizing easier. Space ridges 75 cm apart, matching the standard row spacing for planting. 
### Before Planting ###
 After ridging, wait 3 to 5 days for a first flush of weeds to sprout, then spray a contact herbicide like Paraquat to clear them before you plant. If you have cured poultry manure or cow dung, spread it across the field before harrowing so it mixes into the root zone.

### Choosing Seed ###
 Don't plant grain bought for eating — buy certified, treated seed from a licensed agro-dealer for reliable germination. Open-pollinated varieties like SAMMAZ 14 or 27 are cheaper, drought-tolerant, and can be replanted for up to 3 seasons. Hybrids like Oba Super 9 or Premier 7 yield much more (5–8 tonnes per hectare) but need good fertilizer and fresh seed every season. White maize is preferred in the south for Ogi and Tuwo, while yellow maize is what poultry feed mills in the north want most. 
### When to Plant ###
 Southern Nigeria: early season is late March to mid-April; a shorter late-season planting runs early to mid-August. Northern Savanna: late May to mid-June in the Southern Guinea Savanna, and late June to early July further north in the Sudan Savanna. Too early risks dry spells; too late cuts off water right when the plant is flowering. 
### Spacing and Sowing ###
 Plant seeds 3 to 5 cm deep. Space rows 75 cm apart, and plants 25 cm apart within the row for one seed per hole (or 50 cm for two seeds per hole). You'll need roughly 20 to 25 kg of seed per hectare. 
### Looking After Young Plants ###
 Apply a pre-emergence herbicide within 48 hours of planting, since maize can't compete well with weeds. Hand-weed or spray a selective herbicide later if needed. Apply a basal NPK fertilizer at or shortly after planting, then top-dress with urea around week 5–6 before tasseling. Check the inner leaves weekly for Fall Armyworm — window-like holes or sawdust-like waste in the whorl are early warning signs — and spray promptly if you spot them.

Maize is a heavy feeder and needs a steady supply of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Relying only on chemical fertilizer wears down the soil over time, while manure alone usually can't meet the crop's full nutrient needs — combining both works best.
