### Manure Options ###
 Poultry manure: the richest option in nitrogen and phosphorus, and it releases nutrients quickly for an early growth boost. Cow dung: cheap and widely available, especially up north, and it breaks down slowly for longer-lasting soil improvement. Pig manure: effective, but high in moisture and salt, so it needs to be well composted with dry crop residue first. Compost or green manure: decomposed kitchen waste, leaf litter, or nitrogen-fixing cover crops like Mucuna or cowpea, ploughed back into the soil before planting. 
### Chemical Fertilizer ###
 NPK 15:15:15 or NPK 20:10:10 is the standard basal fertilizer, giving a balanced early mix for leaves, roots, and stalk strength. Urea is used for top-dressing to push vegetative growth and cob formation. It evaporates easily, so it should be buried or applied when the soil is damp. Calcium Ammonium Nitrate (CAN) is a good alternative to urea in acidic southern soils, since it doesn't add to the acidity. Single Super Phosphate (SSP) helps in phosphorus-poor soils, common in the northern savannas, by encouraging deep root growth. 
### A Simple Timeline for One Hectare ###
 2–4 weeks before planting: work 2 to 5 tonnes of cured manure into the soil. 1–2 weeks after seedlings emerge: apply about 6 bags (300 kg) of NPK 15:15:15 or 20:10:10, buried near — not touching — the plant stem. 4–5 weeks after emergence: top-dress with 2 to 3 bags of urea (or CAN on acidic soil), applied when the soil is moist. 7 weeks after emergence: for high-yield hybrids, an optional extra bag of urea just before tasseling helps fill out the ears. Where possible, get a basic soil test before buying fertilizer, so you're not paying for nutrients your soil already has. And avoid applying fertilizer during heavy rain (it washes away) or onto bone-dry soil (it just burns the crop).

Weeds quietly eat into maize profits. If left unchecked, they compete with young plants for sunlight, water, and fertilizer, and can cut yields by 50% to 80%. The first 4 to 6 weeks after planting matter most — once the maize is knee-high, its leaves shade the ground and keep new weeds down. 
### Weeds to Watch For ###
 Spear grass: a tough perennial grass with sharp roots that steal nutrients from maize roots. Siam weed: spreads fast in southern and western Nigeria and can choke young crops. Striga (witchweed): a parasitic weed common in the north that attaches to maize roots underground and drains the plant before it even shows above soil. 
### Using Herbicides ###
 Pre-emergence, within 48 hours of planting: a combination of Atrazine (for broadleaf weeds) and Metolachlor or Alachlor (for grasses), sprayed onto damp soil before the maize sprouts. Post-emergence, 3–4 weeks after planting: a selective herbicide like Nicosulfuron or 2,4-D amine for weeds that got through. Make sure it's labeled safe for maize — never spray Glyphosate over a standing crop, as it will kill the maize too. 
### Manual and Cultural Control ###
 First hand-weeding at 2–3 weeks, second at 5–6 weeks if needed, done carefully to avoid cutting the shallow roots. Intercropping with cowpeas, groundnuts, or egusi melon helps carpet the ground and block sunlight from reaching weed seeds. The stale seedbed trick: prepare the land, wait 1–2 weeks for the first weeds to sprout, spray them with a cheap contact herbicide, then plant without disturbing the soil again. 
### Dealing with Striga ###
 Plant Striga-tolerant maize varieties, such as the SAMMAZ series. Rotate maize with soybeans for a season — soybean roots trick Striga seeds into germinating, but since Striga can't feed on soybeans, it starves before you replant maize.

Planting maize on the same field year after year wears down the soil's nitrogen, builds up pests like Fall Armyworm, and encourages Striga. Rotating with legumes and root crops breaks those cycles and can boost yields by 20–30% compared to growing maize continuously. 
### Good Rotation Partners ###
 Soybeans and cowpeas: the best partners — they fix nitrogen in the soil that the next maize crop can feed on, cutting fertilizer costs. Cassava and yam: deep roots break up compacted soil and pull up nutrients from lower down that shallow maize roots can't reach. Groundnuts and pigeon peas: good cover crops that shade the soil, suppress weeds, and add organic matter. 
### Two Simple Rotation Plans ###
 2-year plan (popular in the north): Year 1 soybeans or cowpeas, Year 2 maize. 3-year plan: Year 1 maize, Year 2 soybeans, cowpeas, or groundnuts, Year 3 cassava or yam. 
### A Few Tips ###
 Don't burn the leftover vines and leaves from your beans or groundnuts — plough them back in so they rot into organic compost for the maize. Avoid rotating maize with sorghum or millet — they're all grasses that share the same pests and drain the same nutrients, so it doesn't break anything. In the south, you can rotate within a single year: maize during the early rains (March–July), followed by cowpeas during the shorter late rains (September–November).

Maize faces pests both while it's growing in the field and after it's harvested and stored. 
### Field Pests ###
 Fall Armyworm: the most feared maize pest in Nigeria — this fast-spreading caterpillar can strip a field almost overnight. Look for ragged, torn leaves, small window-like holes, and sawdust-like waste packed into the center of the plant. Stem borers: native caterpillars that leave small pinholes in young leaves before tunneling into the stalk, causing the top leaves to wither and die (called "deadheart") and weakening the stalk so it snaps easily in wind or rain. 
### Storage Pests ###
 Maize weevil: the main threat to stored maize, capable of reducing a good harvest to empty husks and dust within about three months. Look for tiny round holes in the kernels and a build-up of white powder in the sack. Larger grain borer: an aggressive beetle that tunnels through both grains and cobs, turning them into fine, chalky flour.

### Fall Armyworm ###
 Spray insecticides containing Emamectin Benzoate, Chlorantraniliprole, or Indoxacarb, aiming the spray right into the center whorl of the plant, since that's where the pest hides. Spray early morning (6–8 AM) or evening, since the pest hides deep in the plant during the hot afternoon. Plant early with the first steady rains to get ahead of peak moth activity, and intercrop with cowpeas or groundnuts to confuse egg-laying moths. 
### Stem Borers ###
 Use treated seed (such as a Cyantraniliprole coating) to protect seedlings early on. Try the "push-pull" method: intercrop maize with Desmodium, whose scent pushes borers away, and plant Napier grass around the field edges to pull and trap them. 
### Storage Pests ###
 Dry grain down to 12–13% moisture before bagging — this alone goes a long way toward preventing weevil damage. Clean out old grain residue and dust from the storage room before bringing in a new harvest. Use PICS (triple-layer hermetic) bags to seal out oxygen and suffocate any insects inside without chemicals. For large commercial stores, fumigation tablets sealed under airtight tarpaulin for 7–14 days can be used, but this creates a dangerous gas and should only be handled by trained operators wearing protective gear.

How and when you harvest maize depends on whether you're selling it fresh or as dry grain. 
### Fresh (Green) Maize ###
 Harvested around 50 to 70 days after planting, once the silk turns dark brown and pressing a kernel releases a milky fluid. This is sold quickly to roadside roasters or vegetable markets. 
### Dry Grain Maize ###
 Harvested at 90 to 120 days, once the husks are fully brown and papery, the kernels are hard, and a black layer has formed at the base of the kernel. 
### Picking and Drying ###
 Hand-pick ears by snapping them downward off the stalk, then strip the husks in the field or a clean courtyard. Spread the dehusked cobs on clean tarpaulins or concrete for 3 to 7 days in the sun. Never let cobs touch bare soil directly — soil contact brings in fungi that produce toxic aflatoxins, which make the grain unsellable. 
### Shelling and Winnowing ###
 Shell by hand-crank sheller or by beating cobs in sacks with sticks; larger farms use motorized shellers. Winnow using wind or a fan to blow away chaff and dust, leaving clean grain.

Stored maize in Nigeria mainly has to survive two threats: too much moisture, which causes mold, and the maize weevil. 
### Checking Moisture ###
 Bring grain down to 12–13% moisture before bagging. If you don't have a moisture meter, try the salt test: put dried grain in a dry jar with some kitchen salt, shake it for a minute, and if salt sticks to the sides or the grains, it's still too damp and needs more drying. 
### Safe Storage ###
 Use PICS (hermetic) bags to seal out air and suffocate insects without chemicals — this is the safest option for grain you'll be eating. Avoid mixing in unapproved household chemicals; stick to registered, food-safe protectants if extra treatment is needed. 
### Warehouse Care ###
 Sweep out old grain, dust, and cobwebs before bringing in a new harvest, and treat walls with an approved residual insecticide if needed. Never stack bags directly on a concrete floor — it draws up moisture and rots the bottom bags. Use elevated wooden pallets, and leave a gap between the bags and the walls for airflow.

A tomato is a red, juicy fruit from a flowering plant in the nightshade family, originally from South America. Technically it's a fruit since it grows from a flower and has seeds, but most people treat it as a vegetable because of how it's used in cooking. People eat tomatoes raw in salads and sandwiches, cooked into soups, stews, and sauces, or processed into ketchup, paste, and juice. In Nigeria, tomato farming is often called "Red Gold" — it's a high-stakes business that's central to the way Nigerians cook, but it comes with real risk because prices swing wildly and the supply chain is fragile. Everyday demand: tomatoes go into stews, jollof rice, and soups eaten across the country every day. Big profit potential: when tomatoes are scarce, prices shoot up — a single basket can sell for ₦50,000 to ₦70,000 or more. Fast cycle: from nursery to harvest takes only 3 to 4 months, so farmers can clear and replant quickly. Northern states like Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Jigawa, and Plateau grow most of the country's fresh tomatoes, using dry-season irrigation to keep supply going year-round. In the south, states like Oyo, Ogun, and Lagos are increasingly turning to greenhouse and screenhouse growing to get around the wetter climate. Despite the opportunity, the crop has real challenges — up to half of what's harvested is lost before it reaches consumers due to poor storage, prices crash when everyone harvests at once, and pests like Tuta absoluta (nicknamed "Tomato Ebola") can wipe out a field almost overnight. Nigeria is Africa's second-largest tomato producer, yet still spends heavily every year importing processed tomato paste — which is why many farmers see local processing as the next big opportunity.

Tomatoes aren't native to Nigeria — they arrived through trade during the colonial era and grew into one of the most important ingredients in Nigerian cooking, as well as a major part of the economy. 
### Arrival and Early Adoption ###
 Before tomatoes arrived, Nigerian stews and soups relied on local peppers, palm oil, locust beans, and leafy vegetables. Once colonial traders introduced tomatoes, cooks found they paired perfectly with local peppers, and tomatoes became the base of dishes like Jollof Rice and classic tomato stew. 
### Growing Into a Northern Powerhouse ###
 After independence, farmers and agricultural experts realized the northern savanna states — especially Kano, Kaduna, and Katsina — had ideal soil and climate for large-scale tomato growing. Dams built in the 1970s, like the Tiga Dam in Kano, made dry-season irrigation possible, turning the north into the country's main source of fresh tomatoes. Early processing companies like Vegfru and Tomapep also set up factories during this period to handle surplus harvests. 
### The Import Years ###
 Over time, poor storage infrastructure and unreliable power caused local processing factories to shut down, and Nigeria became one of the world's biggest importers of tomato paste, spending hundreds of millions of dollars a year — even while growing more fresh tomatoes than almost anywhere else in Africa. Around half the harvest was still rotting before it reached anyone, for lack of proper storage. In 2016, an outbreak of Tuta absoluta devastated fields in the north, pushing prices up by over 400% and making tomato scarcity a national concern. 
### Rebuilding Local Production ###
 More recently, the government has tightened import rules on tomato paste and offered low-interest loans to smallholder farmers to encourage local growing. Businesses like Tomato Jos and the Dangote Tomato Processing Factory now work directly with farmers to turn fresh harvests into paste locally. Combined with better hybrid seeds, improved pest control, and new approaches like greenhouse farming in the south, the country has made real progress in smoothing out the price swings that used to hit household budgets so hard.

### Climate ###
 The best temperatures are 21°C to 28°C during the day and 15°C to 20°C at night. When daytime temperatures stay above 35°C, or nights stay above 24°C, the pollen dries out and flowers drop off without setting fruit — this is common in northern Nigeria during March and April. Tomatoes need at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sunlight a day — too little and the stems grow thin and spindly with poor flowering. Moderate humidity (50–70%) is ideal. Higher humidity, common in the south during the rainy season, encourages fungal and bacterial diseases. Moderate, evenly spread rainfall of 600 mm to 1,200 mm a year works best — too much rain splits ripening fruit and washes away nutrients. 
### Soil ###
 Deep, fertile sandy loam or silt loam is ideal — it drains well while letting roots grow up to 60 cm deep. Heavy clay traps water and causes root rot. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH of 6.0 to 6.5. Below pH 5.5 (common in the south), phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium get locked up; above pH 7.5, iron and boron become scarce. Tomatoes can't handle standing water — even 24 hours of it can drown the roots by cutting off oxygen. Soil with 2–3% organic matter or more supports the crop's heavy nutrient needs best. 
### Regional Notes ###
 Northern Savannah (e.g. Kano, Kaduna): plenty of sun and lower humidity means fewer fungal problems, but heat and sandy, low-retention soil are challenges — drip irrigation, heavy manure, and heat-tolerant varieties help. Southern Rainforest (e.g. Oyo, Enugu): good water supply and long growing seasons, but high humidity brings fungal and bacterial wilt, and soils tend to be acidic — agricultural lime, raised beds, and regular fungicide help here.

Good land preparation gives tomato roots loose, well-aerated soil to grow deep into, clears out weeds and soil pests, and improves drainage so roots don't drown during heavy rain. 
### Clearing and Tillage ###
 Clear away weeds, shrubs, old crop residue, and large rocks. Plough 20 to 30 cm deep to break up the hard crust, expose soil pests to the sun, and improve aeration. Harrow to break large clods into a fine, smooth texture, giving young seedling roots better contact with the soil. 
### Beds and Ridges ###
 Build raised beds or ridges 75 to 100 cm apart, 15 to 20 cm high, to prevent waterlogging during the rains and keep soil loose. Work well-rotted poultry manure or cow dung into the top 10–15 cm of the beds, at roughly 10 to 20 tonnes per hectare, at least two weeks before transplanting. 
### Regional Adjustments ###
 In the acidic soils common in southern and eastern Nigeria, apply agricultural lime or dolomite (about 500g to 1kg per 10 square meters) during ploughing to neutralize acidity and prevent blossom-end rot. In the sandy soils of the north, use extra organic manure to help the soil hold onto water and nutrients. Since tomatoes are vulnerable to soil-borne fungal wilts, drenching the beds with a copper-based fungicide, or mixing in beneficial Trichoderma with the manure, helps sanitize the soil before planting.

### Starting Seeds ###
 Sow seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before you plan to transplant, about 6 mm deep in a sterile, moist seed-starting mix, kept at 21°C to 24°C. 7 to 10 days before transplanting, start hardening off seedlings — move them outdoors into partial shade for a few hours a day, gradually increasing sun and wind exposure so they don't go into shock. 
### Transplanting ###
 Pick a spot with 6 to 8 hours of direct sun daily, and work 5 to 10 cm of aged compost into loose, well-draining soil. Bury seedlings deep, up to the top two sets of leaves — the buried stem grows extra roots, giving the plant a stronger, more drought-resistant root system. Space plants 60 to 90 cm apart, with rows about 1.2 meters apart, and install stakes or cages at planting time so fruit and leaves stay off the damp ground. Water 2.5 to 5 cm weekly directly at the soil, keeping the leaves dry, and mulch with 5 to 7 cm of straw or similar material to hold in moisture and regulate soil temperature.

Nigerian soils are often low in organic matter, so getting good tomato yields means combining manure with mineral fertilizer on a set schedule. Manure must be fully cured before use — fresh manure can burn young seedlings. 
### Manure Options ###
 Poultry manure: the richest and most popular choice, high in nitrogen for fast, healthy leaf growth. Cow dung: widely available in the north and west, lower in immediate nutrients but great for conditioning sandy or clay soil and holding water. Pig manure: effective but needs 3 to 4 months of composting to remove harmful pathogens. Compost: made from kitchen waste, dry grass, and neem leaves — helps balance soil pH and improve nutrient uptake. 
### Fertilizer Types ###
 NPK 15:15:15 or NPK 20:10:10 gives a balanced start — nitrogen for leaves, phosphorus for roots, potassium for fruit and water regulation. Urea is used early on for a strong vegetative growth boost. Muriate of Potash or potassium nitrate, applied during flowering and fruiting, increases fruit weight, size, and skin thickness. Calcium nitrate is especially important — calcium prevents blossom-end rot, the black, soft patch that can form on the bottom of the fruit. 
### A Simple Feeding Timeline ###
 At land prep (2 weeks before transplanting): mix about 1 kg of well-composted manure into each planting hole, or spread it evenly across the rows. 14 days after transplanting: apply 2.5g each of NPK 15:15:15 and urea per plant, buried in a shallow ring 5–10 cm from the stem, then water immediately. 28 days after transplanting: repeat the same 2.5g NPK and 2.5g urea dose. 42–56 days (flowering and first fruit set): stop urea, since too much nitrogen at this stage means leafy plants with poor fruit. Apply 2.5g of Muriate of Potash with 2.5g of NPK 15:15:15, and add calcium nitrate to support smooth, unblemished fruit skin. 70–84 days (main harvest window): apply 2.5g of a high-potassium fertilizer every two weeks to keep fruit size up through repeated pickings.

Weeds steal sunlight, water, and nutrients from tomato plants, and can also host pests and fungal disease. A mix of prevention, mulching, and targeted control works best. 
### Prevention ###
 Stale seedbed trick: water the prepared soil 2 weeks before planting to get weed seeds sprouting, then hoe or flame-weed them before transplanting. Rotating with a dense cover crop like velvet beans or alfalfa in the previous season helps choke out weeds ahead of time. Spacing plants so the canopy closes quickly shades the ground and starves new weeds of light. 
### Mulching ###
 A 5 to 10 cm layer of straw, dried grass, or rice hulls around the base of plants blocks light to weed seeds and holds in soil moisture. Black plastic mulch laid over the beds before transplanting, with small holes cut for the plants, suppresses weeds almost completely along the row. 
### Manual and Chemical Control ###
 Hoe shallowly (under 3 cm) on a weekly basis to avoid damaging the tomato's shallow roots, and hand-pull weeds growing close to the stem or cage. A pre-emergence herbicide like Metribuzin or Pendimethalin, applied to bare soil before transplanting, stops weed seeds from sprouting. If needed between rows, selective post-emergence herbicides can be used carefully, with a spray shield to keep chemicals off the sensitive tomato leaves.

Tomatoes are heavy feeders and prone to persistent soil diseases, so rotating them with non-nightshade crops on a 3 to 4-year cycle is important. Rotation helps prevent soilborne diseases like Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, and bacterial wilt. It interrupts the life cycle of root-knot nematodes. Alternating heavy feeders with soil-building plants restores nutrients and organic matter. Switching between deep-rooted tomatoes and shallow-rooted crops helps restore compacted soil layers. 
### A 4-Year Rotation ###
 Year 1: tomatoes. Year 2: beans, peas, or a cover crop to fix nitrogen. Year 3: cabbage, broccoli, or kale (light feeders). Year 4: carrots, onions, or garlic, which help break up the soil. 
### What to Avoid ###
 Don't follow tomatoes with potatoes — they share the same diseases, like late blight. Avoid peppers, which are vulnerable to the same bacterial and viral problems. Avoid eggplants too, since they attract the same insect pests.

Tomatoes attract a wide range of pests, and knowing what damage each one causes makes it much easier to catch problems early. 
### Tomato Leafminer (Tuta absoluta) ###
 A small grey-brown moth whose larvae are the real danger — they burrow into leaves, leaving behind blotchy, transparent patches, and tunnel into stems and fruit, causing rot and, if unchecked, near-total crop loss. This pest is widely feared in Nigeria and nicknamed "Tomato Ebola." 
### Tomato Fruitworm ###
 Also known as the corn earworm. Newly hatched worms head straight for green fruit, chewing deep, messy holes into the stem end and leaving droppings behind — a single worm can ruin several fruits on one branch. 
### Aphids and Whiteflies ###
 Small, soft-bodied insects that gather in colonies under leaves, sucking sap and causing leaves to curl or yellow. They also leave behind a sticky residue that attracts sooty mold, and whiteflies are known for spreading serious plant viruses like Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus. 
### Two-Spotted Spider Mites ###
 Tiny arachnids that thrive in dry, dusty conditions. They puncture leaf cells, causing fine yellow-white speckling, and in large numbers spin webs and turn leaves bronze before they dry up and fall.

### Tomato Leafminer ###
 Use pheromone traps to track and disrupt moth mating, and remove and burn heavily infested leaves. Encourage natural predators like Macrolophus bugs or parasitic Trichogramma wasps to attack the eggs. Because larvae feed inside the plant, use systemic sprays rather than contact ones — rotating between options such as Emamectin Benzoate, Chlorantraniliprole, and Spinosad helps prevent resistance building up. 
### Fruitworm ###
 Use light traps at night to catch adult moths before they lay eggs. Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or NPV weekly starting at flowering — Bt needs to be eaten by the worm before it burrows into fruit. For chemical control, diamides like chlorantraniliprole work better than generic pyrethroids, which fruitworms have grown resistant to in many areas. 
### Aphids and Whiteflies ###
 Hang yellow sticky traps just above the plants to catch flying pests. Protect natural predators like ladybugs, hoverflies, and lacewings by avoiding broad-spectrum chemical sprays. Insecticidal soap or neem oil works well if applied thoroughly, especially under the leaves, since it needs to physically coat the insect. 
### Spider Mites ###
 Keep plants well-watered — dry conditions favor mites, and occasional misting can physically knock them off leaves. Regular insecticides don't work on mites and can even make things worse by killing their predators — use a proper miticide like Abamectin along with horticultural oil instead. 
### General Strategy ###
 Never plant tomatoes or peppers in the same soil back-to-back, and till or solarize the soil between cycles. Use sticky traps and pheromone lures early, before pest numbers build up. Spray biological treatments like Bt or Spinosad in the late afternoon or evening, since strong midday sun breaks them down quickly. Save systemic chemical sprays for when scouting shows pest numbers have actually crossed a damaging threshold, rather than spraying on a fixed schedule.

### When to Pick ###
 Harvest at the "breaker stage" — when the green skin just starts turning light pink or orange on about 10% of the fruit. Tomatoes ripen well off the vine without losing flavor, so there's no need to wait for full red on the plant, especially if rain is coming, since heavy water can split the fruit. 
### How to Pick ###
 Gently snap the fruit off, keeping the small green cap intact — this protects the skin seal and keeps bacteria out. You can also use clean, sharp pruners instead of snapping by hand. Place harvested tomatoes gently into shallow baskets or trays — don't stack them deep, since the weight bruises the fruit underneath. 
### After Picking ###
 Sort out any bruised, cracked, or insect-damaged fruit, and wipe off dry dirt with a clean cloth rather than washing with cold water, which can draw moisture into the stem scar.

### Ripening at Room Temperature ###
 Keep breaker-stage tomatoes indoors, out of direct sunlight, at 18°C to 21°C, in a well-ventilated spot. Lay them in a single layer, stem-side down, so they don't roll or bruise — this lets them ripen evenly using their own natural ethylene gas. 
### Skip the Fridge ###
 Never store fresh, whole tomatoes below 12°C. Cold temperatures permanently damage the compounds responsible for flavor and break down the fruit's texture, leaving it mealy and tasteless. 
### Preserving Extra Tomatoes ###
 Core, peel, and freeze surplus ripe tomatoes for later cooking. Or process them into jars using a safe, high-acid water-bath canning method.

Groundnut is another name for the peanut, a legume whose pods ripen underground rather than on the plant. In West Africa and much of the Commonwealth, "groundnut" is the everyday word for it, though people also call it goober, monkey nut, or potato bean in other parts of the world. In Nigeria, groundnut is a crop that does double duty — it earns farmers cash and feeds the household, and it's especially important in the northern savanna, where it's grown at large scale. Nigeria is Africa's biggest groundnut producer, and for many smallholders it carries both economic and cultural weight. Cheaper to grow: groundnut needs far less fertilizer than crops like maize, which makes it attractive to smallholders working with limited budgets. Two income streams: farmers sell the kernels for eating, snacks like Kulikuli, and oil, and they can also sell the haulms (the dried stalks and leaves) as valuable livestock feed. A source of pride: groundnut is tied to Nigeria's history through the famous Kano Groundnut Pyramids from the years before the oil boom, and many farmers see today's revival of the crop as a way back to that era. As a legume, groundnut fixes its own nitrogen in the soil, which makes it a valuable partner in crop rotation with cereals. It grows especially well in the semi-arid conditions of states like Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Bauchi, Borno, and Plateau. The main challenges farmers face are disease — especially Groundnut Rosette Disease — and aflatoxin contamination, which is why disease-resistant varieties like SAMNUT 24 and SAMNUT 30 have become so important.

Groundnut has a dramatic history in Nigeria — from a local food crop to the backbone of the national economy, then a near-total collapse, and now a slow return to prominence. 
### Becoming a Cash Crop ###
 Groundnut had been grown as food for centuries before the British colonial administration turned it into a major export crop in the early 1900s, mainly to supply European soap and oil mills. Everything changed in 1912, when the Kano-Lagos railway was completed, making it possible to move huge volumes of groundnuts from the northern savanna down to the port in Lagos for shipping. 
### The Birth of the Pyramids ###
 In 1919, a merchant named Alhassan Dantata, a major supplier to the Royal Niger Company, came up with a distinctive way to store groundnuts — stacking 50 kg bags into massive pyramids, with a single pyramid sometimes holding up to 15,000 bags. 
### The Golden Era ###
 By the 1950s and 60s, groundnut had become Nigeria's most valuable single export, and the country was producing over 41% of West Africa's total output. The pyramids in cities like Kano became famous landmarks, appeared on postage stamps, and turned into a genuine source of national pride, with the revenue funding infrastructure and creating a class of wealthy local traders. 
### The Collapse ###
 By the late 1970s, the pyramids had vanished. Several things happened at once: the discovery of oil in the Niger Delta shifted government focus away from agriculture, and the marketing board that had organized groundnut pricing was dissolved. Severe droughts in 1972–73 wiped out fields, and a major outbreak of Groundnut Rosette Disease in 1975 destroyed millions of hectares. Production fell from over 1.6 million metric tons to less than 0.7 million tons within a decade, and many farmers switched to safer crops like cowpea, sorghum, and millet. 
### Where Things Stand Today ###
 The physical pyramids are gone, their old sites now used for buildings and football fields, but Nigeria has quietly become Africa's largest groundnut producer again, and one of the top producers globally. The focus today has shifted from colonial-era exporting to feeding local demand for peanut oil, livestock feed, and snacks like Kulikuli.

### Climate ###
 The best temperatures are 22°C to 30°C. Below 20°C slows growth and delays germination, while above 35°C can reduce flowering and pod formation. Groundnut needs 500 mm to 1,000 mm of well-spread rainfall per season. Moisture matters most at germination and during flowering/pegging, but the crop needs dry weather in the final 3 to 4 weeks before harvest — rain at that stage rots pods, causes early sprouting, and encourages mold. The crop needs strong sunlight — clear, sunny days help it branch more, flower more, and build up more oil in the kernels. 
### Soil ###
 Well-drained sandy loam, loamy sand, or alluvial soil is ideal. Loose soil lets the "pegs" (the stalks that grow down from fertilized flowers) easily push into the ground to form pods, and makes harvesting clean and easy. Avoid heavy clay — it holds too much water, causing rot, and hardens when dry, trapping pods underground during harvest. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH of 5.5 to 7.0. Below pH 5.0, the Rhizobium bacteria the plant needs for nitrogen fixing can't survive. Good calcium levels in the top 5–10 cm of soil (the podding zone) are important — low calcium causes "pops," pods that look fine outside but are empty or have shriveled kernels. 
### Regional Suitability ###
 Sudan/Sahel Savanna (e.g. Kano, Katsina): excellent — ideal rainfall, plenty of sun, and naturally sandy soil. Early-maturing varieties work best here. Guinea Savanna/Middle Belt (e.g. Benue, Niger): very good, though ridges are needed to manage seasonal waterlogging. Southern Rainforest Zone: only marginal — rainfall and humidity are too high, raising the risk of foliar disease, pod rot, and poor drying conditions.

Because groundnut pods form entirely underground, the soil needs to be loosened properly so pegs can penetrate easily and pods can be lifted cleanly at harvest. 
### Clearing ###
 Clear weeds, grasses, and shrubs, and dig out tree stumps and roots — leftover roots damage tractor or ox-plow equipment, and decaying wood left in the field attracts termites that go on to attack the pods. 
### Ploughing and Harrowing ###
 Plough 20 to 30 cm deep soon after the first steady rain, once the soil is moist but not sticky. This breaks up the hard crust, buries weed seeds, and exposes soil pests to birds. Harrow afterward to break large clods into a fine, crumbly texture — clumpy soil traps air pockets that dry out seeds and blocks pegs from entering the ground later. 
### Ridges or Flat Beds ###
 In the Middle Belt and southern zones (e.g. Benue, Niger, Kwara), build ridges 50 to 60 cm apart to improve drainage, keep the root zone aerated, and prevent pod rot from waterlogging. In the drier Sudan and Sahel Savanna (e.g. Kano, Katsina, Sokoto), flat beds work better, since they help conserve scarce soil moisture. 
### Working in Fertilizer ###
 Spread 5 to 10 tonnes of fully rotted cow dung or compost per hectare before the final harrowing or ridging so it blends into the soil. If using Single Super Phosphate, apply it during final seedbed preparation so it sits right where the young roots will grow.

### Seed Selection ###
 Avoid using grain bought from the open market as seed — go for certified seed that resists Groundnut Rosette Virus and leaf spot disease. SAMNUT 30 is a strong performer, high-yielding, good for livestock fodder, and resistant to rosette disease. SAMNUT 24 and 26 mature early (90–100 days), good for northern areas with shorter rains. SAMNUT 22 and 14 (Yar Dakarkari) mature medium to late and suit the Guinea Savanna, with high oil content. Treat kernels with an antifungal/insecticide seed dressing (such as Dress Force or Apron Plus) before planting to protect against soil pests, rot, and birds. 
### Timing ###
 Southern Rainforest zone: plant March/April for an early crop, or August/September for a late crop. Middle Belt: plant April/May. Northern Savannas: plant June/July. 
### Spacing and Depth ###
 Plant seeds 3 to 5 cm deep. Bunch/erect types: 10 cm between plants, 50 cm between rows. Spreading types: 15 cm between plants, 60 cm between rows. 
### Early Care ###
 Groundnut fixes its own nitrogen, so at planting the focus is on Single Super Phosphate for phosphorus and calcium — calcium especially helps prevent "pops." Weed early, since the crop can't compete well with weeds in its first 6 weeks — but stop all hoeing once flowering and pegging start, usually 25–35 days in, since hoeing at that point severs the pegs entering the soil.

Because groundnut fixes its own nitrogen through root nodules, fertilizer for this crop is mostly about phosphorus, calcium, and potassium — nutrients that build heavy pods, prevent empty shells, and boost oil content. 
### Manure ###
 Apply well-rotted cattle dung, poultry manure, or compost, broadcast 2 to 3 weeks before ploughing and harrowing so it has time to integrate, at a rate of 5 to 10 tonnes per hectare. Never use fresh, undecomposed manure — it brings in weed seeds and pests like termites and white grubs, and can burn young seedlings. 
### Phosphorus ###
 Single Super Phosphate (SSP) is the preferred choice, since it also supplies sulfur and calcium. Apply 150 to 200 kg per hectare as a basal dressing, either broadcast during final land prep or banded along the ridges just before planting. 
### Calcium ###
 A calcium shortage causes "pops" — pods that look normal outside but are empty or have shriveled kernels inside. Apply agricultural gypsum (200 to 400 kg per hectare) at flowering/pegging time, about 25–40 days after planting, broadcast over the plants so it washes into the top 5 cm of soil where pods develop. 
### Potassium ###
 Muriate of Potash improves kernel weight and oil quality. Apply 40 to 60 kg per hectare alongside the phosphorus at planting, if a soil test shows it's needed. 
### Nitrogen — Just a Starter ###
 Since groundnut fixes its own nitrogen, heavy nitrogen fertilizer actually works against the crop, pushing leafy growth at the expense of pods. On very poor soil, a small starter dose of 20 to 30 kg of urea or NPK 15-15-15 per hectare at planting can help the plant along until its root nodules form around day 21. One rule matters throughout: never apply soil-disturbing fertilizer once pegs have started entering the ground, and always apply fertilizer to damp soil, since dry soil causes nutrient loss and root burn.

Groundnut struggles against weeds, especially in its first 3 to 6 weeks. Left unmanaged, weeds can cut yields by 30% to 70%, both by competing for light, water, and nutrients and by physically blocking pegs from reaching the soil. 
### The One Rule to Remember ###
 Never use a hoe or heavy tool once flowering and pegging begin, usually 25–35 days after planting — mechanical weeding at that stage cuts the pegs entering the ground. Any weeding needed after that point should be careful hand-pulling only. 
### Cultural and Manual Control ###
 Thorough ploughing and harrowing before planting buries existing weeds and delays new ones from emerging. Planting at the recommended close spacing helps the canopy close quickly, shading out weed seeds. If weeding by hand, do the first round at 2–3 weeks and the second at 5–6 weeks after planting. 
### Herbicides ###
 Pre-emergence, within 24–48 hours of planting: Pendimethalin controls grasses and some broadleaf weeds, while Butachlor or Metolachlor targets grasses and sedges. Spray onto moist soil before the groundnuts sprout. Post-emergence, for grasses that escape early control (around 3–4 weeks in): selective grass killers like Quizalofop-p-ethyl or Fluazifop-p-butyl can be sprayed directly over the canopy. Post-emergence, for broadleaf weeds: Bentazon works, but only if applied early while weeds are still small (2–4 leaf stage).

Rotating groundnut with other crops breaks disease cycles, reduces nematodes, manages weeds, and makes the most of the nitrogen groundnut leaves behind in the soil. 
### Good Partners ###
 Cereals (maize, sorghum, millet): heavy nitrogen feeders that benefit from what groundnut leaves behind, while also disrupting the aphids that spread Groundnut Rosette Virus and other foliar diseases. Root and tuber crops (cassava, yam): their deep roots tap nutrients from lower soil, and groundnut does well in the loose soil left behind after they're harvested. Some cassava varieties even help suppress root-knot nematodes. Cotton: works well in a 3-year rotation in the Sudan and Guinea Savanna zones, and helps prevent groundnut-specific pathogens from building up. 
### What to Avoid ###
 Other legumes like cowpea, beans, or soybeans — they share the same pests and diseases, including root rot and root-knot nematodes, which multiply quickly if legumes are grown back to back. Tomatoes and peppers, which can host bacterial wilt that also attacks groundnut. 
### Sample Rotations ###
 Northern Savanna (Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Borno): Year 1 groundnut, Year 2 sorghum or pearl millet, Year 3 cotton or maize, then back to groundnut. Middle Belt/Southern Guinea Savanna (Benue, Niger, Kwara, Kogi): Year 1 yam or cassava, Year 2 groundnut, Year 3 maize, then back to groundnut. 
### Good Habits ###
 Plough leftover groundnut vines and roots back into the soil after harvest — they break down into organic nitrogen for the next cereal crop. Never grow groundnut on the same land two seasons running — it builds up pests fast and drains micronutrients like boron and calcium.

Left unchecked, pests can destroy an entire groundnut harvest in Nigeria. They attack above ground, below ground, and after harvest in storage. 
### Groundnut Aphids ###
 Small black insects that cluster on shoots, leaves, and flowers, sucking sap and causing wilting. Their bigger danger is that they're the only carrier of Groundnut Rosette Virus, which stunts the plant, puckers and discolors leaves, and can wipe out the whole yield. 
### Thrips ###
 Tiny slender insects that feed inside buds and on young leaf surfaces, scraping tissue and causing leaves to curl and scar. They also spread viruses like bud necrosis. 
### Foliar Caterpillars ###
 Armyworms and leaf miners that chew leaves and bore into stems, reducing the plant's ability to photosynthesize. 
### Termites ###
 A major threat during dry spells across the Nigerian savannas. They attack roots and stems from below, and scrape at mature pods underground, weakening the shells and letting in fungi like Aspergillus flavus, which produces dangerous aflatoxins. 
### White Grubs ###
 The C-shaped larvae of scarab beetles, living entirely underground. They eat fine roots and sever taproots, causing sudden patches of wilting plants, and chew ragged holes into developing pods. 
### Groundnut Bruchid ###
 The most destructive pest after harvest. The female lays eggs on the pod shell, and the larvae bore through into the kernel to feed, emerging as adults and leaving clean, round exit holes — reducing good nuts to powder.

### Aphids ###
 Plant early with the onset of rains so the crop develops before aphid numbers peak, and use close spacing to help the canopy close quickly, since aphids prefer open, sparse stands. Spray systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid, Lambda-Cyhalothrin, or Dimethoate at the first sign of aphids. 
### Thrips ###
 Use resistant varieties like SAMNUT 22 or 30. Spray contact or systemic insecticides if numbers cross a damaging threshold (roughly 5 thrips per terminal bud). 
### Caterpillars ###
 Hand-pick on small plots; for larger farms, use contact insecticides like Cypermethrin or a Bt-based spray. 
### Termites and White Grubs ###
 Harvest promptly once mature — leaving pods in dry soil invites termite attack. Deep ploughing exposes termite tunnels and grubs to predators, and helps keep manure fully decomposed before use, since fresh manure attracts egg-laying beetles. Soil-applied insecticides or a seed dressing containing Thiamethoxam before planting also helps against termites. 
### Groundnut Bruchid ###
 Dry pods thoroughly to under 7% moisture before bagging. Store in hermetic (PICS) triple-layer bags to suffocate the insects without chemicals. For conventional jute bags, fumigate the warehouse with Aluminium Phosphide tablets under gas-tight tarpaulin if needed.

Groundnut is usually ready 110 to 150 days after planting. Harvesting too early gives shriveled kernels with low oil content, while harvesting too late risks pods breaking off in the soil or sprouting if rain falls. 
### Checking Maturity ###
 Pull up a few plants at random and crack open the pods. If the inside of the shell is white, the crop isn't ready. Once 70–80% of the inside shells have turned dark brown or black, the crop is mature and ready to harvest. 
### Lifting the Plants ###
 If the soil is dry and hard, wait for a light rain or apply light irrigation to loosen it first. Use a hand hoe or tractor-drawn digger to loosen the root zone, then gently lift the whole plant so the pods stay attached to the vines rather than breaking off underground. 
### Field Curing ###
 Shake off excess dirt and invert the plants in rows with the pods facing up toward the sun and breeze, letting them air-dry for 3 to 5 days.

### Stripping and Final Drying ###
 Once dry, hand-pick or mechanically strip the pods from the vines. Spread them on clean tarpaulins or concrete — never bare soil — and continue drying until moisture drops below 7–8%. You'll know it's ready when the seeds rattle loudly inside the shell and the pod snaps easily under thumb pressure. 
### Safe Storage ###
 Store groundnut unshelled whenever possible — the shell acts as a natural barrier against insects and moisture. Pack clean, dry pods into breathable jute bags, or use hermetic airtight bags for shelled kernels to suffocate pests without chemicals. Stack bags on elevated wooden pallets, away from concrete floors and walls, in a cool, well-ventilated, rodent-proof room.

Cocoa is the dark brown powder made from the crushed seeds of the tropical Theobroma cacao tree. The tree grows large, colorful pods, each holding 30 to 50 seeds wrapped in a sweet pulp. Once harvested, the seeds are dried, roasted, and ground into a paste, then pressed to remove most of the fat, leaving behind the powder used to make chocolate and cocoa drinks. In Nigeria, cocoa is far more than a crop — it's the country's leading agricultural export, and it directly supports the livelihoods of over 300,000 smallholder farmers, mostly across the southern rainforest belt. Family heritage: most Nigerian cocoa farmers work small plots inherited from their parents and grandparents, and being a cocoa farmer is a deep part of identity in southwestern states like Ondo, Osun, and Oyo. The "school fees" crop: because the main harvest (October to February) brings a large cash payout, families rely on it to cover tuition, build houses, and pay medical bills. High-value returns: cocoa connects local farmers to international pricing, so when global prices surge — as they did dramatically in 2024 — farmers can access a level of income other local crops can't match. It's also demanding work. Cocoa can't easily be mechanized — farmers prune by hand, harvest pods with sickles, crack them open, and spend days turning beans in the sun to ferment and dry. The rainforest climate makes crops vulnerable to fungal disease like Black Pod, and many farmers are working with trees 25 to 30 years old that simply don't produce as much as younger ones. On top of that, newer export rules like the EU's deforestation regulation now require farmers to digitally map their land to prove it isn't on deforested ground, in order to keep access to European buyers.

Cocoa's story in Nigeria runs from a colonial experiment to a global economic powerhouse, and then through a long period of neglect that the country is still working to recover from. 
### First Trials ###
 Cocoa was first brought to Nigeria in 1874, with early experimental farms in Bonny and Calabar, but the soil and climate there weren't suited to it. A breakthrough came in 1880 when a farm succeeded in Lagos, and by the 1890s farmers in Abeokuta, Ibadan, and Egbaland were planting it in their rainforests, where it thrived and spread quickly through Ilesha, Ondo, Ife, and Ekiti. 
### The Colonial Boom ###
 Cocoa quickly grew into a major cash crop and helped build a prosperous, educated Yoruba middle class who could send their children abroad to university. Farmers mostly grew Amelonado cacao from Brazil, alongside a red Trinidad variety. In 1947, the British set up the Nigeria Cocoa Marketing Board to standardize quality and organize exports to the UK and North America. 
### The Golden Age ###
 By independence in 1960, Nigeria was the world's second-largest cocoa producer, behind only Ghana, producing over 200,000 metric tonnes a year. Under the Western Regional Government led by Chief Obafemi Awolowo, cocoa revenue funded Africa's first free primary education program, the continent's first television station, and the University of Ife. In 1965, Cocoa House was completed in Ibadan — at 105 meters, it was West Africa's first skyscraper, built entirely from cocoa, rubber, and timber money. 
### The Oil Shift and Decline ###
 In the 1970s, the discovery of crude oil pulled government attention away from agriculture. Young people moved to the cities, and thousands of cocoa plantations were abandoned. Nigeria's ranking slipped from second to fourth in the world, and today the country produces around 340,000 metric tonnes a year, behind Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, and Indonesia. 
### Today's Revival ###
 With global cocoa prices surging in recent years, government and private investors are working to revive old plantations, bring in climate-resistant seedlings, and help Nigeria reclaim more of its historic standing in the industry.

### Climate ###
 Cocoa needs 1,500 mm to 2,500 mm of rain a year, well spread across the wet season. It can handle a dry season, but not longer than 3 to 4 months — beyond that, trees shed leaves and drop pods. Best temperatures run 18°C to 21°C at the low end and 30°C to 32°C at the high end. Below 15°C stunts growth, and above 35°C scorches leaves and dries out flowers. Cocoa thrives on high humidity, ideally 80–90% during the day, rising to 100% at night — though too much humidity combined with poor pruning invites Black Pod disease. Young seedlings need 50–70% shade, while mature trees do best with 30–40% dappled shade, from scattered taller trees or plantains. Strong, dry winds — like the Harmattan blowing from the Sahara between December and February — strip leaves and dry out flowers, so windbreaks along farm borders are worth having. 
### Soil ###
 Deep, well-drained loamy or clay-loamy soil is ideal, at least 1.5 meters deep with no hard rock layers, so the taproot can anchor and reach water during the dry season. The soil needs to hold moisture without waterlogging — heavy, compacted clay causes root rot and yellowing leaves. Ideal pH is 6.0 to 7.5. Below 5.5, common in heavily weathered rainforest soil, phosphorus and calcium become hard for the tree to absorb. The top 15–30 cm of soil should be rich in organic matter, with good levels of potassium, calcium, and magnesium to support pod development. 
### Where Cocoa Grows Best in Nigeria ###
 The core zone: southwestern states like Ondo (the largest producer), Osun, Oyo, Ekiti, and Ogun, plus Cross River (the second-largest producer), Edo, and Delta — all with deep rainforest soils and consistent rain. Marginal areas: parts of Kwara, Kogi, and the Mambilla Plateau in Taraba, where farmers need extra irrigation, windbreaks, and mulching to help trees survive longer dry seasons.

Getting land ready for cocoa is less about deep tilling and more about protecting the soil and setting up the right shade conditions from the start. 
### Choosing the Site ###
 Look for humid rainforest zones with 1,200 to 2,000 mm of rain a year, in states like Ondo, Cross River, Osun, Oyo, or Ekiti. Go for deep, well-drained, fertile loamy soil with a pH between 5.0 and 7.5. Choose gentle slopes with good natural drainage — avoid waterlogged valleys or exposed, dry hilltops. 
### Clearing ###
 Clear shrubs, stumps, and unwanted trees by hand or machine, but avoid heavy, deep ploughing or bulldozing — that strips away organic matter and disturbs the soil life cocoa depends on. Minimal disturbance is the goal. 
### Setting Up Shade ###
 Plant fast-growing temporary shade crops like plantains or bananas ahead of time, since young cocoa seedlings need protection from direct sun. Keep or plant permanent shade trees, such as oil palm or Gliricidia, spaced evenly to manage canopy cover as the cocoa matures. 
### Laying Out and Digging Holes ###
 Mark planting rows at a standard 3m x 3m spacing, giving roughly 1,100 to 1,200 trees per hectare. Dig planting holes about 30 cm x 30 cm x 30 cm, 4 to 6 weeks before transplanting. Mix the dug-out soil with compost or well-rotted manure and refill the holes ahead of the rainy season.

### Seeds and Nursery ###
 Use fresh seeds from healthy, disease-free ripe pods, and plant them right away — they lose the ability to sprout within days of leaving the pod. Raise seedlings in small polythene bags of rich soil under a shaded canopy, watering daily for 3 to 4 months until they're sturdy enough to transplant. 
### Transplanting ###
 Move seedlings to the field at the start of the rains (April to June), spaced roughly 3 meters by 3 meters. Because young trees are very sensitive to direct sun, intercrop them with fast-growing food crops like bananas, plantains, or cocoyams for temporary shade. Traditional trees take 3 to 5 years to bear their first pods; modern hybrid varieties can start producing in as little as 2 to 3 years.

Since a cocoa tree can stay productive on the same land for 30 years, it draws heavily on soil nutrients over time — good fertilizer management is what keeps yields up and plantations healthy. 
### Chemical Fertilizer by Stage ###
 Years 1–2 (seedlings and young plants): NPK 15:15:15 gives balanced nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, often paired with Single Super Phosphate to boost early root growth. Year 3 onward (mature, fruit-bearing trees): a high-potassium NPK blend, such as 12:12:17 with added magnesium, replaces what pods strip from the soil while keeping leaves healthy. Potassium sulphate is preferred over chloride-based potassium, since it fills out beans well without harming the plant. 
### Organic Options ###
 Cured poultry manure has been shown to boost seedling height and stem thickness. Decomposed cow dung mixed with dry leaves gives a slow, steady release of nitrogen and organic matter. Chopped-up empty cocoa pod husks left to rot around the trees recycle a good amount of natural potassium back into the farm. Fresh manure should never touch cocoa roots directly — it generates heat as it breaks down and can burn the roots, so it needs to be fully dried and composted first. 
### How and When to Apply ###
 Apply fertilizer once the rains are properly established (May to July) — too dry and it scorches roots, too wet and it washes away. Use the ring method: clear weeds and bury fertilizer in a ring 15 to 30 cm from the trunk, right under the edge of the leaf canopy where the feeding roots are. Liquid foliar fertilizers sprayed onto leaves in the cool morning are increasingly used to boost flowering and protect young pods.

Weeds compete with cocoa for water, nutrients, and sunlight, and heavy weed growth traps humidity at ground level, which encourages Black Pod disease and gives pests like mirids and rodents somewhere to breed. How you manage weeds depends heavily on whether the farm is young and open, or mature with a closed canopy. 
### Young Farms (Years 1–3) ###
 Weed pressure is high since sunlight reaches the ground freely. Grasses like spear grass and Siam weed can quickly choke young seedlings. 
### Mature Farms (Year 4+) ###
 Weed pressure drops since the tree canopy blocks light naturally. The main issue becomes soft broadleaf weeds and vines trapping humidity around the lower trunk. 
### Manual Control ###
 Ring weeding: clear a 1-meter circle around each young seedling so it has exclusive access to nutrients and fertilizer. Strip slashing: cut down weeds in the paths between rows using a brush cutter or cutlass. Never scrape the soil bare with a hoe near the trunk — cocoa has shallow feeding roots close to the surface that heavy hoeing can slice, opening the door to root disease. 
### Cover Crops and Mulching ###
 Planting legume cover crops like Mucuna pruriens or Centrosema between rows chokes out grasses while adding nitrogen to the soil for free. Mulching with dry grass, banana leaves, or empty pod husks around (not touching) the trunk blocks weeds and holds in moisture, especially useful heading into the dry season. 
### Herbicides ###
 On young farms, use gentler contact herbicides like Glufosinate-ammonium rather than systemic ones, and shield seedlings with a guard or plastic cover while spraying — young green stems easily absorb and are damaged by strong chemicals. On mature farms, Glyphosate can be used carefully along paths, since the woody bark doesn't absorb it easily. Always spray with the nozzle pointed down, and never on windy days.

Since cocoa is a tree that stays on the same land for decades, it can't be rotated the way seasonal crops are. Instead, farmers use a system of intercropping and agroforestry that cycles different food crops through the farm as the cocoa tree grows — achieving many of the same soil and pest benefits over time. 
### Before Planting ###
 Farmers plant fast-growing plantain, banana, or papaya 4 to 5 months ahead of the cocoa, to keep the soil damp and shade the coming seedlings from harsh midday sun. 
### Years 1–3: Growing Food Alongside Young Cocoa ###
 First year: maize and melon — melon spreads fast, chokes weeds, and protects topsoil from heavy rain. Second year: yams, cocoyams, or cassava, which loosen the soil. Alongside these: cowpeas, which fix nitrogen into the soil for the young cocoa roots. This gives the farming family food and income while they wait years for the cocoa to bear its first pods. 
### Years 4–5: Closing Canopy ###
 Once the cocoa branches meet overhead and the ground gets too dark for crops like maize, farmers phase out the annual food crops and thin out the plantains and papayas — too much shade at this point risks Black Pod disease. 
### Year 5 Onward: Mature Agroforestry ###
 The farm settles into a permanent, layered system: scattered tall trees like oil palm, kola nut, citrus, or African walnut form a high, pruned canopy giving dappled light, while the mature cocoa grows underneath, feeding off the nutrient-rich leaf litter falling from above. 
### Rules to Keep In Mind ###
 Keep to the 3m x 3m grid for cocoa, and plant intercrops in the middle of the rows so they don't compete with cocoa roots. Avoid heavy cassava planting in year one, since it can rob young cocoa of soil moisture during the dry season. Never leave empty pod husks piled near tree bases — compost them away from the trees to avoid spreading fungal spores.

Pests can cause yield losses of 25% to 45% on Nigerian cocoa farms if left unmanaged. Three pests cause most of the damage. 
### Cocoa Mirids (Capsids) ###
 Known locally as "Bana-bana" or "Akalamigbo," mirids are the single most destructive cocoa pest in Nigeria, responsible for up to 30% of national yield losses. They pierce stems, shoots, and pods with a needle-like mouth and inject toxic saliva as they feed, killing tissue and leaving sunken black lesions. These lesions can merge and dry out whole branches — a condition called "Capsid Blast" — and also let in fungal spores that cause deep wood rot. Mirids peak between August and October. 
### Cocoa Pod Borer ###
 A tiny, hard-to-spot moth that lays eggs on the surface of green pods. The larvae tunnel into the husk and feed on the sweet pulp inside, causing beans to clump together, turn black, and die — a normal-looking pod can end up hollow and full of insect waste instead of usable beans. 
### Mealybugs ###
 Small, white, waxy insects that gather on shoots, flowers, and pod stalks, sucking sap and stunting growth. Local ants often "farm" them for their sweet honeydew and protect them from predators. Their real danger is that they're the only carrier of Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus, which causes stem and root swelling, leaf distortion, and kills the tree within 2 to 5 years — there's no cure, so an infected tree has to be uprooted and burned.

### Cultural and Mechanical Control ###
 Prune to keep tree height under 4 meters and thin the canopy to allow 30–40% dappled sunlight through — this reduces the humidity mirids and pod borers need to breed. Do a sanitation sweep every 7 to 10 days during peak harvest, removing any pod showing signs of borer damage or disease. Encourage weaver ants in the canopy — they aggressively hunt and kill mirid nymphs, caterpillars, and pod borer moths (though workers should wear protective clothing during harvest, since these ants bite). Never crack pods inside the farm — move them to a clearing, and bury the empty husks in pits covered with lime or soil to stop them attracting pests. 
### Organic and Biological Control ###
 A neem oil spray (about 50ml pure neem oil and 10ml mild liquid soap in 10 liters of water) acts as a natural anti-feedant — mirids and caterpillars that taste it stop eating and starve. Beauveria bassiana, a beneficial fungus, can be applied as a biopesticide that targets pod borer larvae without harming the surrounding environment. 
### Chemical Control ###
 Use CRIN-approved systemic insecticides like Imidacloprid or Thiamethoxam, which are absorbed into the plant and poison sap-sucking pests like mirids and mealybugs from within. Avoid unapproved or broad-spectrum chemicals — they can leave residues that get shipments rejected by export buyers. Two sprays a year target the main mirid surge: one in August/September as trees flush new growth, and a follow-up in October/November, 4 to 6 weeks later, to clean up survivors before harvest. Never spray within 30 days of a planned harvest — residue on the beans can get entire export shipments rejected.

Cocoa harvesting is done entirely by hand, since machines would damage the trees. Harvest peaks twice a year — the main crop from October to February, and a smaller light crop from May to August. 
### Picking Ripe Pods ###
 Ripe pods change color — green pods turn bright yellow, and purple pods turn deep orange. Cut the pods with a sharp machete for low ones, or a long hooked knife on a bamboo pole for high branches. Cut the stalk cleanly without damaging the bark, since future pods grow from the same spot. 
### Breaking the Pods ###
 Within a few days of picking, crack the pods open with a wooden club or blunt tool — sharp knives risk nicking and damaging the seeds inside. Scoop out the wet, sticky pulp and seeds into baskets or onto banana leaves.

The chocolate flavor cocoa is known for doesn't exist in the raw bean — it's created entirely through fermentation and drying after harvest. 
### Fermentation (5–7 Days) ###
 Pile the wet beans on banana leaves or in wooden boxes and cover tightly with more leaves. Over the week, natural yeasts and bacteria break down the sugary pulp, generating heat up to 50°C, which kills the seed and develops the chocolate flavor and aroma. Turn and mix the beans every 48 hours for even fermentation. 
### Sun Drying (7–10 Days) ###
 Spread fermented beans in thin layers on raised wooden platforms or bamboo mats in the sun, raking regularly for even drying. This brings moisture down from around 60% to a safe 7%. Drying too slowly invites mold; drying too fast makes the beans brittle and bitter. 
### Sorting and Bagging ###
 Pick out flat, broken, or insect-damaged beans along with stones and debris, then pack the good beans tightly into breathable jute bags. 
### Warehouse Storage ###
 Store bagged beans in a clean, well-ventilated warehouse, stacked on elevated wooden pallets rather than directly on the concrete floor, so they don't draw up moisture and spoil.

Millet is a group of small-seeded cereal grasses grown mostly in hot, dry regions of Africa and Asia. It's one of the oldest crops humans have grown, prized for surviving harsh heat, drought, and poor soil with very little water. Some varieties mature in as little as 60 to 90 days, and the grain is naturally gluten-free and rich in protein, fiber, iron, calcium, and B vitamins. Pearl millet: the most widely grown type, especially across West Africa and India. Finger millet: common in East Africa, known for its high calcium content. Foxtail millet: grown mainly in Asia for food and animal feed. Proso millet: often used in birdseed mixes and health foods. For farmers in Nigeria's dry north, millet is a genuine lifeline. It grows where crops like maize would fail, needs little fertilizer or water, and matures fast enough to feed a family before other crops are ready. Staple food: families use it for thick porridges like tuwo, and drinks like kunu and fura. Hunger breaker: because it's ready early, it fills the gap when stored food from the last season is running low. Extra value: nothing goes to waste — the stalks feed animals, build fences, or serve as cooking fuel. Income: farmers sell surplus grain locally, and processing companies buy it for flour and commercial drinks.

Millet's history in Nigeria stretches back over 4,000 years, making it one of the oldest crops grown on Nigerian soil — unlike rice or wheat, which arrived from elsewhere. 
### Ancient Roots ###
 Pearl millet was first domesticated in the Sahel region of West Africa around 2500 BC. Archaeologists have found thousands of charred pearl millet seeds at Nok culture sites in central Nigeria dating back to 1500 BC, showing it was a core food for some of Nigeria's earliest organized societies. From West Africa, trade routes eventually carried the grain as far as South Asia. 
### The Millet Belt ###
 Over centuries, millet growing became concentrated in Northern Nigeria — modern-day Bornu, Yobe, Kano, Sokoto, and Katsina — because of its ability to survive harsh Sahelian droughts. Early farmers developed intercropping, growing millet alongside sorghum and cowpea, so that if the rains failed and other crops died, millet would still pull through. Over time, local seed selection produced three distinct Hausa varieties still used today: Gero (fast-maturing), Maiwa (late-maturing), and Dauro (transplantable). 
### Part of the Culture ###
 Millet became deeply woven into the food culture of northern and central Nigeria, forming the base of dishes like Fura da Nono (pounded millet balls with fermented milk), Tuwo Gari, and the popular drink Kunu Zaki. 
### Decline and Comeback ###
 During the colonial era and much of the 20th century, government focus and funding shifted to export cash crops like groundnut and cotton, and to imported grains like rice and wheat, pushing millet to the sidelines. In recent decades, though, climate change and rising food costs have driven a real revival. Today Nigeria is Africa's leading millet producer and third in the world, with the grain shifting from a "poor man's food" into a valued, climate-smart health food.

### Climate ###
 Millet grows best in the Sudan and Sahel Savanna zones of northern Nigeria — states like Borno, Yobe, Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, and Jigawa. It can grow in the Guinea Savanna (Middle Belt) too, though excess rain there risks root rot. It needs surprisingly little water — 400 mm to 800 mm across the season is ideal, and fast-maturing Gero varieties can produce a harvest on as little as 250 mm. Best temperatures are 25°C to 35°C, and it can tolerate heat up to 40°C during early growth — conditions that would kill most other cereals. It needs full, unshaded sunlight — strong sun speeds up grain filling and helps the crop mature quickly. 
### Soil ###
 Sandy loam, loamy sand, or alluvial soil is ideal — loose enough for the fibrous roots to dig deep in search of moisture. Drainage is critical — millet has zero tolerance for standing water. A field waterlogged for more than a few days will suffocate the roots and kill the plant. Ideal pH is 5.5 to 7.0, though millet tolerates moderately alkaline soil better than most cereals, and also handles low fertility and higher salinity better than maize. Avoid heavy clay soils (like Vertisols or Fadama land) — they trap water and crust over, stopping the tiny seeds from sprouting. On sloped land, build ridges across the slope rather than up and down, to stop heavy rain from washing away the shallow-planted seeds.

Because millet seeds are so small, poor land preparation easily leads to patchy germination or seeds buried too deep. Land can be prepared with a tractor, oxen, or manual hoes depending on what's available. 
### Clearing ###
 Clear weeds, shrubs, and stones during the dry season. If millet or sorghum grew on the field the previous season, pull up and partially burn or bury the old stalks — this destroys stem borer larvae that hide inside over the dry months. Light weeds and leaves can be worked into the soil instead of burning, to build up organic matter. 
### Working in Manure ###
 Apply 3 to 6 tonnes of well-decomposed cow dung or poultry droppings per hectare in the late dry season (around April/May), just before ploughing, so it gets mixed deep into the root zone. 
### Ploughing and Ridging ###
 Plough 15 to 20 cm deep right after the first stable rain softens the ground — this breaks the hard crust and improves water infiltration. If using a tractor, harrow afterward to break clods into a fine, even seedbed. Build ridges 75 cm apart — they improve drainage, make weeding easier, and on sloped land, contour ridging (across the slope) helps prevent erosion. 
### Minimum Tillage Option ###
 In areas with fragile, sandy soil prone to wind erosion, like parts of Yobe or Borno, some farmers skip ploughing entirely and instead dig small planting holes directly into undisturbed soil at the usual 75 cm spacing. This keeps the soil covered and traps moisture, protecting it from being blown away.

### Choosing a Variety ###
 Gero (pearl millet): the most popular in Nigeria, highly climate-resilient, and fast-maturing at 60–90 days — good for shorter rainy seasons. Maiwa and Dauro: later-maturing (120–150 days); Dauro is unusual in that it's raised in a nursery first, then transplanted. 
### Timing ###
 Plant at the start of the rains, usually May to June in northern Nigeria. 
### Sowing ###
 Sow seeds shallow, 2 to 3 cm deep — planting too deep stops the tiny seeds from sprouting. Space rows 75 cm apart, with 25 to 30 cm between plants within the row. Use about 4 to 5 kg of seed per hectare for even coverage. 
### Early Care ###
 Thin to 2–3 strong plants per stand within 2 weeks of germination — leaving too many crowds the roots and produces thin stalks and small heads. Weed early — millet can't compete with weeds in its first month. Do the first weeding at 2–3 weeks, the second at 5–6 weeks after planting.

Millet is resilient enough to grow on poor sandy soil, but proper feeding can double or triple a traditional harvest. A mix of organic manure and mineral fertilizer works best. 
### Manure ###
 Cow dung is the most commonly available option; poultry droppings release nitrogen faster and are especially potent. Apply 3 to 6 tonnes per hectare, broadcast evenly during dry-season land prep, then ploughed or harrowed into the soil before ridging. If manure is limited, apply it as a thin band along the bottom of planting furrows instead of broadcasting it across the whole field. 
### Mineral Fertilizer ###
 Basal application (at planting or 2 weeks after emergence): NPK 15-15-15 or NPK 20-10-10 at about 4 bags (200 kg) per hectare, placed 5 cm from the plant and 5 cm deep — never touching the stem directly. Top-dressing (4–5 weeks after planting): 1 to 1.5 bags (50–75 kg) of urea per hectare, applied when the soil is moist. Avoid over-applying nitrogen late in the season, since it produces weak stalks that fall over in wind. 
### Micro-Dosing ###
 Because fertilizer can be expensive for smallholders, a widely promoted technique in northern Nigeria is micro-dosing — dropping a small pinch (about 2–3 grams) of NPK directly into the planting hole or next to the root, instead of spreading it across the whole field. This can cut fertilizer costs by roughly half while making sure the roots get nearly all the nutrient before weeds can steal it.

Millet's tiny seeds mean seedlings grow slowly for the first 3 to 4 weeks, leaving them vulnerable to weeds — yield losses of 30% to 80% are possible if weeds go unmanaged. 
### Striga (Witchweed) ###
 Known locally as Inna or Kaddara, Striga is a parasitic weed that attaches to millet roots and drains water and nutrients before it even shows above ground, leading to yellowing leaves, twisted stems, and empty seed heads. A single plant can drop up to 100,000 seeds that stay viable in the soil for over 15 years, making it one of the toughest weeds to deal with. 
### Manual Weeding ###
 Keep the field clean for the first 4 weeks — after that, millet's canopy shades out most new weeds on its own. First weeding at 2–3 weeks (often combined with thinning), second at 5–6 weeks, when soil is also piled up around the base of the plants to help stabilize the stalks against wind. 
### Other Cultural Methods ###
 Stale seedbed trick: let the first rain sprout hidden weed seeds, then plough them under before sowing millet. Intercropping with cowpeas or groundnuts creates a low, flat canopy that blocks light from reaching weed seeds. Rotating with soybean or groundnut tricks Striga seeds into sprouting without letting them attach to a host, starving the weed out over time. Heavy organic manure boosts soil nitrogen, which helps millet resist Striga's attack. 
### Herbicides ###
 Pre-emergence, within 48 hours of planting: a mix of Atrazine and Metolachlor on damp soil creates a barrier against sprouting weed seeds. Post-emergence, for broadleaf weeds or young Striga shoots: 2,4-D or Triclopyr, applied once millet is 3–4 weeks old, using a deflector nozzle to keep the spray low and away from the plant's center leaves.

Rotating crops is a low-cost way to break pest cycles, manage weeds, and keep soil fertile without relying entirely on fertilizer. Growing millet on the same field every year drains nitrogen fast and cuts yields. 
### The Core Idea ###
 Follow millet, a heavy feeder, with a nitrogen-fixing legume, which leaves a natural fertility boost behind for the next millet crop. 
### A Simple 2-Year Cycle ###
 Year 1: cowpea or groundnut. Year 2: millet. Research shows this pairing raises nitrogen availability and boosts millet yields compared to growing millet continuously. 
### A Fuller 3-Year Cycle ###
 Year 1: cowpea or soybean, to fix nitrogen into the topsoil. Year 2: millet, feeding on the nitrogen left behind. Year 3: a deep-rooted crop like sweet potato, cassava, or a different cereal like sorghum, pulling up nutrients from deeper soil that millet's shallow roots can't reach. 
### Why It Matters ###
 Fighting Striga: legumes like cowpea and groundnut act as trap crops — they trick Striga seeds into sprouting, but since the weed can't attach to legume roots, it starves and dies, clearing the field naturally. Breaking pest cycles: stem borers and head caterpillars hide in dry millet stalks over the dry season — planting a non-cereal crop next starves them out. Feeding livestock: in states like Borno, Yobe, and Kano, rotating with cowpea also produces nutrient-rich cowpea hay, a valued dry-season feed for cattle, sheep, and goats.

Left unmanaged, pests can cause millet yield losses ranging from 20% to over 80% in Nigeria. 
### Millet Stem Borer ###
 The most destructive and widespread millet pest across northern Nigeria. Caterpillars bore into the stem after hatching, disrupting water and nutrient flow. In young plants, this causes "dead heart" — the central shoot wilts and dies. In older plants, weakened stems snap or fall over in wind, and seed heads come out stunted and grainless. 
### Millet Head Miner ###
 A major threat during flowering in the drier Sahelian belt. Eggs are laid directly on the green millet heads, and hatching caterpillars burrow in to eat developing seeds, leaving spiral tracks and heavily damaged, nearly empty heads. 
### Shoot Fly ###
 An early-season pest that attacks seedlings within their first two to three weeks. Larvae crawl into the shoot to feed, causing the same "dead heart" symptom as stem borers and often forcing farmers to replant. 
### Blister Beetles and Chafer Beetles ###
 These arrive in swarms right as millet begins to flower, feeding on pollen, flowers, and the milky immature grains. A field can lose its entire flowering stage within days even though the rest of the plant looks fine.

### Cultural Practices ###
 Plant early with the first stable rains so the crop matures past its most vulnerable stages before pest numbers peak. Burn or bury old millet stalks after harvest rather than using them for fencing near the farm — stem borer larvae hibernate inside them and will hatch right next to the new crop otherwise. Rotate with non-cereal legumes like cowpea or groundnut to starve out cereal-specific pests. 
### Biological Control ###
 Push-pull system: intercrop millet with Desmodium, whose scent repels stem borer moths, and plant Napier grass around the field edge to attract and trap them — the grass's sticky sap kills larvae that bore into it. A homemade neem seed or leaf wash, soaked in water and sprayed on young panicles, is an effective, free way to repel blister beetles and head miners. Conserving natural predators like the Habrobracon hebetor wasp, which preys on head miner caterpillars, helps keep populations down. 
### Chemical Control ###
 Treat seed with an insecticidal dust before planting to protect seedlings from shoot flies and soil pests for the first 21 days. For severe outbreaks of blister beetles or armyworms, spray Cypermethrin or Lambda-Cyhalothrin early morning or late evening, when the air is calm.

Millet is usually ready 60 to 90 days after planting, depending on variety. Don't rely on the calendar alone — check the grain heads directly. 
### Signs of Maturity ###
 The green fades from the seed head, and the grains turn cream, gray, or light brown. A small black spot (the hilum) appears at the base of the grain. The seeds feel hard when bitten. 
### Cutting and Drying ###
 Cut the seed heads with a sharp knife or sickle. Spread the cut heads on clean mats or concrete under the sun for 3 to 5 days until crisp and brittle, before attempting to remove the grain. 
### Threshing and Winnowing ###
 Beat the dried heads with sticks or run them through a mechanical thresher to separate grain from chaff, then dry the loose grain for another 2 days to clear any hidden moisture. Winnow using wind or a mechanical blower to remove dust and light debris, and sieve to sort out stones and broken seeds.

Post-harvest loss is one of the biggest threats to a millet farmer's profit, so getting storage right matters. 
### Checking Moisture ###
 Never bag millet above 12% moisture. If you don't have a moisture meter, use the bite test — a grain should crack sharply between your teeth. If it feels chewy or crushes, it's still too wet and at risk of mold. 
### Choosing Bags ###
 Hermetic (PICS) bags are the gold standard — they suffocate insects and weevil eggs by sealing out oxygen, keeping grain safe for 12 to 24 months without chemicals. If using breathable jute or woven bags instead, treat them with a food-safe insecticide dust to prevent weevils. 
### Warehouse Storage ###
 Stack bags on raised wooden pallets — concrete floors draw up moisture that can rot the bottom layer. Leave at least 50 cm between the stacks and the walls for air circulation. Keep the storage room cool, dark, dry, and well-ventilated, with mesh screens on any openings to keep out rodents and birds while still letting hot air escape.

Ginger is an underground rhizome — not a root, technically, but the swollen underground stem of the plant. It belongs to the same family as turmeric and cardamom, and takes about 8 to 10 months underground to fully mature. It thrives in hot, humid places with rich, loose, well-drained soil. Culinary use: flavors food, tea, baked goods, and drinks around the world. Medicinal use: used traditionally to help digestion and settle an upset stomach. Economic use: a major export crop for countries like India, China, and Nigeria. For Nigerian farmers, especially in Southern Kaduna, ginger has long been the crop that changes a family's fortunes. The "school fees" crop: farmers rely on the ginger harvest to pay tuition, build homes, and secure their livelihood. High risk, high reward: a hectare can cost ₦3.5–4 million to set up, but a good season can yield 10 to 15 tonnes. A path out of poverty: unlike crops grown mainly for the household table, ginger has historically been one of the fastest ways for a farming family to build wealth. Nigerian ginger is known globally for its intense pungency and high oleoresin oil content, which made it a favorite of international buyers — at one point, nearly 90% of what was grown was exported. In recent years, though, fungal blight outbreaks fueled by rising temperatures have wiped out up to 90% of harvests for many farmers, driving up seed prices and pricing Nigerian ginger out of the export market for a period.
